## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 — Lean: CP chapters 3, 7, 11 (+ notes 30–40), 16, 17 close; ep02/draft Ambrose cites verified; UP chapters skimmed

## Top findings for Cardinal
1. **Where "late May" comes from** (CANON-133):
   - Ambrose cites the "hardest blow" sentence to E. B. Crocker's letter of **May 27, 1867** (ch. 11 n. 34, p. 397).
   - His own narrative then follows letters of June 26 and 28 and has Charles confront the strikers on **July 1 "after a week"** (¶54–57). That fits Chang's Monday, June 24 start.
   - **Fixed** the documentary draft, which had credited Ambrose for the June 28 dating.
2. **Provisions** (CANON-134): Ambrose has Charles Crocker cutting off provisions (¶57). Chang has E. B. crediting the Chinese headmen at the time. The drafts already follow Chang. Logged as a dispute.
3. **Ten-mile day** (CANON-135; ch. 16 ¶36–49, pp. 347–350):
   - The $10,000 bet; the April 27 derailment postponed the attempt.
   - Sunrise 7:15 a.m. Corinne time; six miles by the 1:30 meal; ten miles fifty-six feet by 7 p.m.
   - Eight named Irish rail handlers; spikes "put in place by the Chinese."
   - **Fixed** ep02's "Seven in the morning, a whistle" (all copies). **Rewrote** the ledger 1869-04-28 note with the actual cite (it had said "EPUB not re-opened") and refined its framing.
4. **Promontory** (CANON-136; ch. 17 ¶40–50, pp. 363–365): the gold spike was tapped into a pre-drilled hole. "Stanford swung and missed, striking only the rail. It made no difference." The draft quotations (documentary l.1465, moments.md) are verbatim. This confirms CANON-091 against Rayner and Winkler.
5. **Smaller checks:**
   - Verified: CP incorporated June 28, 1861, and "combined wealth, *according to Huntington*, was $159,000" (ch. 3 ¶48). ep02 now attributes the figure to Huntington.
   - Verified: Crocker's pistol and "bold front" (ch. 2); "almost identical device to the Crédit Mobilier" (ch. 5 ¶18); Strobridge "I will not boss Chinese" (ch. 7 ¶21); six to twelve inches a day (ch. 9 ¶60); Mrs. Strobridge, "the only white woman" (ch. 14 ¶82); Malvern Hill, "a thousand dead and three thousand wounded" (ch. 3); the Lexington's 202 days with Sherman aboard (ch. 2).
   - ep02's "so cut off" corrected to Ambrose's "so isolated" (ch. 2 ¶44, p. 52).

## Do not import from Ambrose
- "In late May … the Chinese went on strike" (ch. 11 ¶52).
- Charles Crocker cutting off provisions, as a contemporaneous fact (¶57).
- Ambrose's tone on the Chinese ("unbelievably and unacceptably"; "not militant"; ¶38 "We are the world"). moments.md already flags the framing as dated.

# Cardinal close reading – Brechin, Imperial San Francisco

**Citation scheme:** print pages from UC Press ebook page anchors [[p. N]] + ¶; endnotes [nN] by chapter.

**Book:** Gray Brechin, *Imperial San Francisco: Urban Power, Earthly Ruin*, with a new preface (Berkeley: University of California Press, ©2006; California Studies in Critical Human Geography 3). Ebook ISBN 9780520933484; pbk ISBN 978-0-520-25008-6. Cardinal Drive (folder 01).

**Clean extract.** UC Press ebook (clean XHTML, not OCR). Working text extracted locally for search (not published). The ebook carries **print page anchors**, rendered as [[p. N]], so we **cite print pages** plus ¶ within each section. Endnotes appear as [nN] and are keyed by chapter in the NOTES section.

**Method.** Every section was read paragraph by paragraph. Yale/East Coast crossover beats are tagged **[IVORY]** and gathered in “Ivory crossovers” at the end.

---


## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 — All: front matter, 2006 preface, 1999 preface/intro, chs 1-7 pp. 1-330, notes pp. 331-357, Note on Sources pp. 358-359

## Front matter
- p. vii: epigraph, H. Robert Braden, *Sunset*, July 1899, “Imperial San Francisco from her hundred hills.”
- Acknowledgments pp. xvii–xix: the book began as a U.C. Berkeley Geography dissertation (Richard Walker, Michael Johns, Christine Rosen). It had a Bancroft Fellowship, and Bill Domhoff and Barton Bernstein are thanked. Mel Scott sent Brechin to Venice in 1985.

## Preface to the 2007 edition (pp. xxi–xxvii, signed March 2006)
- p. xxi: Friedman epigraph: “The hidden hand of the market will never work without a hidden fist … the hidden fist that keeps the world safe for Silicon Valley’s technologies to flourish is called the U.S. Army, Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps.” (n1 Lexus and the Olive Tree, 373)
- p. xxii: W. R. Hearst, 1885, advised his father to invest mining millions in real estate: “Every atom of humanity added to the struggling mass means another figure to [the landlord’s] bank account.” (n3 → ISF p. 68). Brechin planned an *Imperial Manhattan* sequel on Western mining fortunes building New York. **[IVORY] West-to-East capital flow.**
- p. xxiii: the University of California’s first president, **Daniel Coit Gilman**, told the university after 1898 that “Warfare has been changed and [locally made armaments] have shown that it is possible to win great victories overseas … without the sacrifice of the victor’s blood,” and advised it to develop “better means of remote control.” (n8 → p. 291) **[IVORY] Gilman = Yale (verify Bones).**
- p. xxiv: Aug. 15, 1913: M. de Young and W. R. Hearst bought the Spreckels *Call*. Aug. 6, 1999: the de Youngs sold the *Chronicle* to Hearst.
- **p. xxv ¶19–20 (Bechtel + university + weapons):** *Chronicle* “Bay to Baghdad” series: “billions of dollars pouring into the Bay Area economy every year from the Defense Department.” “Silicon Valley continues to be the Pentagon’s laboratory for weapons of the future” (n14, Mar. 20, 2005). **“Three days before Christmas of 2005, the Chronicle announced that the Department of Energy had renewed the university’s contract to jointly run with Bechtel Corporation the Los Alamos laboratories ‘more like a business whose product is nuclear weapons.’”** (n15, *SF Chronicle*, Dec. 22, 2005). The editorial: “worth up to $512 million, but its greater importance to UC is the scientific prestige” (n16, Dec. 23, 2005). **Bechtel–UC–weapons link; verify the LANS contract dates (awarded Dec. 21, 2005; began June 1, 2006).**
- p. xxvi–xxvii: FDR’s Second Bill of Rights (Jan. 11, 1944) as the alternative to the “ethos of mining.”

## Preface “The Urban Maelstrom” (pp. xxix–xxxiv) and Introduction “New Romes for a New World” (pp. 1–9)
- Thesis (p. xxxi–xxxii): the city “does nothing of its own accord … it is driven.” “Linked dynastic elites … through their control of information” make city and contado “collective tools to perpetuate and expand its wealth and power … they can all agree that the city must grow—and its land values rise—to assure the continuation of their dominion.” The “Pyramid of Mining” is introduced (p. xxxii). **Frame for Cardinal: land values + information control + dynastic elites.**
- p. xxxi: *contado* = the territory a city dominates and draws upon. SF land area ≤47 sq mi since 1856, population never above 800,000 (p. xxxiii).
- Intro pp. 1–9: Reagan’s 1985 second inaugural vs. the acid-rain decay of Washington’s monuments. Leutze’s *Westward the Course of Empire Takes Its Way* (Capitol). Frémont named “Chrysopylae (golden gate)” after Byzantium’s Golden Horn (p. 5). George Berkeley’s 1726 line; Seward 1850 (“the perpetual unity of the Empire”); Perry 1856 (p. 7). C. B. Watson 1920: the “star of empire” only “fill[ed] the coffers of the already overrich” (p. 9, n4). Peripheral as facts; useful as rhetoric. Berkeley’s Bermuda college failed “for lack of funds” (p. 7). [IVORY: Berkeley later endowed Yale; not stated by Brechin.]

## Ch. 1 “The Pyramid of Mining” (pp. 13–70)
- pp. 13–16: Pioneer Monument (Thanksgiving 1894) paid for by the James Lick bequest (Lick: “real estate magnate,” fortune “in urban real estate,” p. 15). Irving M. Scott (Union Iron Works) opened the ceremony. The trustees moved the mining figure ahead of agriculture. “Commerce follows the flag … but the flag follows the pick” (p. 15–16).
- pp. 16–22: Mumford’s “Megamachine” as a pyramid. Base: mechanization, metallurgy, militarism, moneymaking. Apex: mining (p. 19). SF motto “Gold in Peace, Iron in War” (p. 16). Classical precedents (Laurium, Rio Tinto: 40,000 slaves; *damnatio ad metalla*). Context only.
- pp. 22–25: Fuggers. The financier who bribed the Imperial Electors for Charles V. **[IVORY]** p. 24–25: “Rothschilds … Rockefellers and Guggenheims developed their own global reach from the new Augsburg of New York.”
- pp. 25–28: Agricola’s *De Re Metallica* (1556): the “detractors” passage, “there is greater detriment from mining than the value of the metals” (Brechin’s emphasis, p. 25). [HOOVER: the Hoovers’ 1912 translation is the standard English; check whether Brechin cites it → see later sections/notes.] Rio Tinto revived by Rothschild capital (p. 26). Railroad “came out of the mine” (p. 27).
- pp. 29–30: the “James Marshall myth.” Washington knew of California’s gold before the war. Larkin to Buchanan, May 4, 1846 (n9). Polk, Dec. 5, 1848 (n10). *California Star*: Yerba Buena “destined to be the Liverpool or New York of the Pacific.”
- **p. 31–32 (LAND):** placer bonanza brief. “The real fortunes were made by city-based financiers in hardrock mercury mining, by commission merchants, and, above all, by those speculating in land and engaging in fraud on an epic scale.” **“The monopolization of land by whatever means necessary laid the foundations for dynastic wealth. For those who’d gotten land cheap or free, there could never be too many immigrants to boost the value of the Golden State’s real estate.”** (n13). Gold peak $81M in 1852; $445M in 1848–58.
- p. 31: Society of California Pioneers (1850), membership restricted to pre-1850 arrivals: a self-made *ancien régime*.
- p. 33: capital channeled “from Eastern and European cities” into flumes [IVORY: Eastern capital]. Hydraulicking (Matteson, Connecticut, 1853). SF foundries supplied pipe: “Iron begot gold.”
- pp. 34–36: hydraulic networks. 5,726 mi of flumes and ditches within a decade; $30M in ditches by 1882. Irving M. Scott: boulders “jump twenty feet in the air,” while “the real hydraulic mine presents a wild and desolate appearance” (p. 36). Fig. 9 caption: these were “not enterprises of the independent miners … but rather required city-based banks and exchanges to raise capital.”
- pp. 36–38: SF Stock and Exchange Board formed Sept. 11, 1862, the first U.S. mining exchange. Brokers were the “Forty Thieves.” 1,300 mining companies within a year, “most of them fraudulent.” The Exchange channeled US and European capital. *Chronicle* 1876: SF wealth “levels the forests.”
- **pp. 38–43 (Ralston’s Ring):** Bank of California (1864). Ralston invited **Darius Ogden Mills** as “titular president” for “probity.” “All of the bank’s directors were heavily involved in mining.” By 1868 the Ring controlled the Exchange (p. 38–39). William Sharon was the Ring’s agent in Virginia City: he “devoured mines, mills, business associates, transportation, judges, legislators, and Sierra timberlands” (p. 39). Ralston also funded “political and judicial bribery.” **Huntington to Hopkins: “I think time will show that Ralston has got a larger institution than he is able to run”; Ralston’s code name for Huntington was “Hungry” (p. 39).** Ralston/Sharon/Mills built a vertical Comstock monopoly (mines, mills, railroad). Insider information let them manipulate the market (p. 41). Stevenson: the Exchange was “a great pump … pumping up the savings of the lower quarters into the pockets of the millionaires upon [Nob Hill]” (p. 41).
- p. 39: George Hearst’s sixth interest in the Ophir launched “a dynasty.”
- p. 43: Comstock output ~$350M over 25 years. Only five mines paid more in dividends than they collected in assessments. Alexander del Mar: the Lode “cost five times what it added to the economy” (n14). South-of-Market foundries had >1,000 men by 1861.
- pp. 44–48: Tahoe/Sierra deforestation. Grant H. Smith: 600M ft of lumber and 2M cords of firewood by 1880. “The graveyard of the Sierra forests.” Sharon acquired timberlands “for the Bank Crowd” as a way “to secretly siphon profits away from the mines” (p. 44).
- **p. 48: “in the infamous winter of 1862, Governor-elect Leland Stanford had to be rowed from his home to his inauguration.”** (Sacramento flood; verify; widely reported Jan. 10, 1862.) North Bloomfield (Ralston, 1866): >$1M, 47 mi of ditch, 8,000-ft tunnel.
- p. 48–49: the profit-takers wore “broadcloth and stovepipes”; “Gold and silver acted as fertilizer to San Francisco’s real estate values.”
- pp. 49–53: Bayard Taylor (*New York Tribune*) poems. Anti-Debris Society (1878) sued in federal court through “an absentee landowner living in New York” (Woodruff). **Sawyer decision Jan. 7, 1884** (permanent injunction against North Bloomfield). Brechin: it “merely confirmed the rights attached to one form of real estate over another” (p. 51). The industry moved abroad. SF dredges (Risdon, Union Iron Works).
- **pp. 53–58 (mining engineers; Hoover; IVORY):** Rickard: the profession is “the herald of empire.” Clubs: “Cosmos, Metropolitan, or Bohemian Clubs” (p. 53). **John Hays Hammond: “With the possible exception of fellow Californian Herbert Hoover, he was the most famous and highly paid engineer of his time”** (p. 53–54). Colleagues called his autobiography “full of lies” (n18, Spence 324, 336). Born SF 1855, moved to New York “to be near abundant capital.” Family friends with **D. O. Mills**, who took Bank of California/Comstock/Tahoe winnings to New York and built the Mills Building at Wall and Broad, “favored by mining companies and engineers” (p. 54). **n19: Mills’s daughter married Whitelaw Reid (*NY Tribune*). “Mills’s son, Ogden, married into the landed aristocracy of the Hudson River valley and his son became Herbert Hoover’s secretary of the treasury”** (Ogden L. Mills). The Mills and Hammond families financed Milham Exploration. **[IVORY ×3; HOOVER.]** Hamilton Smith (North Bloomfield) formed the London Exploration Co. with Rothschild backing (1886). “Californians were managing half the mines on the Rand.” Hammond worked for Barnato and Rhodes. His flogging quote (n23). He ran guns before the Boer War, was jailed in Pretoria, then went to Siberia and to Mexico “for the Mills and Guggenheim families.” Taft’s adviser, kept off the vice-presidential ticket by Guggenheim ties. Mansion in DC, estate at Gloucester, Mass. (p. 56). He lived in a “tight nexus of exclusive clubs, schools, resorts.” [Hammond = Yale Sheffield 1876; Brechin mentions only Freiberg, p. 55. Verify.]
- **p. 58: “By 1912, when Henry and Lou Hoover translated and republished his book …”** **ERROR in Brechin: the translator was Herbert C. Hoover (with Lou Henry Hoover), not “Henry.”** Cross-check Whyte (CANON-017, De Re Metallica). Log it as do-not-import.
- pp. 58–59: “Deferred costs.” DeGroot 1871 on “wrecks of stranded enterprise.” Valley critics said benefits drained to “capitalists based in San Francisco, London, Paris, and New York.” 1882 estimate: the public paid $2–5 for every $1 the mine owners pocketed.
- pp. 59–61: North Bloomfield reported >$2.8M profit, 1866–84. Mines were “close corporations” hiding inside information. G. K. Gilbert (USGS, 1905–09): 1.5 billion cubic yards of sediment, ~8× the Panama Canal excavation. The Corps of Engineers shifted the costs “from assessments on the mining companies, to the farmers, to the taxpayer” (p. 61). **State power absorbing private costs.**
- pp. 61–63: New Almaden (Santa Clara Valley) mercury. ~800,000 cu yd of roasted cinnabar dumped, “permanently poisoning the streams of the western Santa Clara Valley and San Francisco Bay” (p. 62). Comstock lost >7,000 tons of quicksilver. Oakland banned smelters (1870). **UC professor W. J. V. Osterhout told the *Chronicle* in 1906 that smelter fumes were not harmful.** The university as industry consultant (p. 63). The Guggenheims’ 1908 smelter plan was opposed by Hillsborough/Burlingame mining men.
- pp. 63–64: Olmsted (in California 1863–65): SF populated by “thriftless, fortune-hunting … vagabonds”; “there is no society.” Norris, *The Octopus*: ranchers “worked their ranches as … they had worked their mines”; “After us the deluge.”
- pp. 64–67: transfer technology. Hallidie (wire rope → cable car, Aug. 1, 1873, Nob Hill). “Those who financed the cable lines extended them into whatever dune field they had already … bought cheap” (p. 65). Real estate + transit. **Hallidie was a UC Regent; the Regents named the Hallidie Building (1917) for him** (p. 66).
- pp. 67–70: “Financial districts as inverted minescapes.” Deidesheimer square set → skyscraper. D. O. Mills turned mining profits into “vertical rental property on downtown lots” (p. 67). **Hearst to George Hearst, 1885: “The landlords are always a wealthy class. Every infant born in a country makes their land more valuable … every atom of humanity added to the struggling mass means another figure to his bank account”** (p. 68, n31). Land-value doctrine stated outright.

## Ch. 2 “Water Mains and Bloodlines” (pp. 71–117)
- Epigraph: *SF Chronicle* editorial, Aug. 6, 1989: “Economic growth … depends on population growth. Population growth depends absolutely on guaranteed … supplies of good quality drinking water.”
- p. 71: “Power veils itself … elite families marry to agglomerate wealth … they share a common interest in obtaining water to increase the value of their land.” Method: use engineers’ memoirs to trace power.
- pp. 72–73: Sunol Water Temple (Willis Polk, 1910) for William B. Bourn II, who bought Spring Valley in 1907 to sell it to the city “at a handsome profit.” Bourn inherited the Empire Mine and attended Cambridge University. [IVORY-adjacent: English elite education.]
- pp. 73–75: Roman aqueducts and Frontinus (context).
- **p. 76 (STATE POWER → LAND):** in 1858 George Ensign got **the power of eminent domain from the legislature** for private municipal water companies. It “gave the men who ran the pioneer water companies, like those who ran the railroads, the opportunity to acquire virtual empires of real estate.” Spring Valley was “nearly as hated by its own customers as the Southern Pacific.” **“California’s water companies served as the chief instruments for land speculators”** (n1).
- p. 77: 1856 consolidation shrank SF to 47 sq mi and created San Mateo County, “six times larger.” City leaders “wanted San Mateo back.” Plutocrats’ estates on old ranchos (the Howards).
- pp. 77–79: von Schmidt’s Pilarcitos diversion (water arrived July 4, 1862). Lake Tahoe & SF Water Works scheme (1865), mainly to supply hydraulic mines and raise land values along the route. Nevada resisted. William Stewart proposed a Tahoe national park (1900).
- pp. 79–80: Hermann Schussler, Spring Valley engineer for 50 years and consultant to capitalists. His villa sat between the Parrott and Howard estates. **Schussler “advised and insisted upon the timely acquisition of 100,000 acres of increasingly valuable watersheds, reservoir sites, water rights and rights of way”** (p. 80). Crystal Springs Dam sits on the San Andreas Fault.
- pp. 80–84: Ralston hired Olmsted. Olmsted proposed a drought-tolerant linear park (Van Ness valley) but also sold parks by real estate: Central Park adjacent property rose “1,000 percent in only five years” (p. 81). The park was meant to legalize squatter claims and “quiet contested land titles” (p. 81). The city hired William Hammond Hall (Golden Gate Park, 1871–76). Hall’s cousins were **John Hays Hammond** and Richard Pindell Hammond Jr. (surveyor general; president of the park commission) (p. 82). Hall in *Overland Monthly*, 1873: “Water is required for some large city, and forthwith an area many times as great is robbed of its rivulets and brooks—and its fertility” (p. 84, n4). [Cardinal cross-ref: Olmsted later laid out the Stanford campus, 1886–88. Not in Brechin.]
- pp. 85–86: Schussler’s Virginia City siphon (July 29, 1873). Flood: “Everything can be done nowadays; the only question is—will it pay?” Ralston’s Palace Hotel was meant to sell a land scheme south of Market. Ralston, Mills and Sharon built “an intricate financial web … in which money and assets could be moved about secretly, to their private enrichment” (p. 86). **Spring Valley “consistently bribed the very city supervisors required by law to supervise it.”** 1870: ~$480,000 distributed from $816,859 revenue = 59% (n5).
- pp. 86–89: Ralston bought Alameda Creek rights and Spring Valley, using bank certificates priced above the stock’s value. He sold his Alameda rights to the company for a $900,000 profit (n6). He planned to sell the company to the city for $5M profit. The Palace cost nearly 3× its estimate. The supervisors refused.
- **pp. 89–91 (Bank of California crash, Aug. 26, 1875):** Sharon dumped Comstocks, starting the run. Ralston owed the bank nearly $5M. Mills swore “we were all amazed and astonished and grieved.” Ralston drowned. Sharon: “Best thing he could have done” (n7). **Sharon’s “sack-bearers” had bribed his Senate election in Nevada** (n8). Sharon and Mills recast Ralston as a philanthropist. The widow got $50,000. Sharon took the Palace, Belmont, Burlingame Park and Spring Valley control. Flora Sharon married Lord Fermor-Hesketh; Frederick married a Tevis.
- **pp. 92–93 (FIELD):** the Sharon–Hill case. Judge Deady: “property and position are in themselves some certain guaranty of truth” (n13). **Field’s ruling came amid evident conflicts: “Sharon had, after all, loaned Field large sums of money and reserved a complimentary suite for him at the Palace Hotel … while defense counsel Newlands had endorsed his 1884 presidential bid.”** Hill shouted, “How much did Newlands pay you?” Terry was killed by Field’s bodyguard (1889). **Corroborates White (CANON-056): Field took favors from the railroad and banking elite.**
- **pp. 93–95 (Newlands; IVORY):** Newlands married Clara Sharon (1873) and became lead trustee of the Sharon estate. He lost the 1887 Senate bid to George Hearst and moved to Nevada in 1888: “I ought to identify myself politically as a means of influence in matters and litigation relating to the Estate” (p. 93–94). The estate’s Nevada holdings were “second only to those of the Central Pacific Railroad, with which he was closely connected.” He married the niece of **Ward McAllister** (New York society). **“the Yale-educated blue blood”** (p. 94). He developed **Chevy Chase** (1,720 acres, Maryland) from Dupont Circle lands bought with Stewart. Burlingame, “the Tuxedo Park of the West” (R. P. Hammond Jr.), then **Hillsborough (1910), “one of the nation’s premier power centers,” like “the men’s clubs of Nob Hill and the Bohemian Grove”** (p. 94).
- pp. 95–97: second generation “marrying European titles and one another.” **“Phantom capital”:** private trusts and estate companies form “an informal economy as invisible to the public as the black market,” run by family lawyers, chief among them Newlands (p. 96–97).
- pp. 97–98: Secrecy. N. W. Aldrich, *Old Money* (n18): the patriciate held “complete domination of all educational and cultural institutions … exceptionally favored treatment at the hands of political and civic officers … All these assets were hereditary.” Office “often proves highly lucrative in the service of phantom capital seeking to tap the public treasury for private gain” (p. 97). Brechin does not note the Stanford link; verify before use.] PG&E power.

Rockefeller’s son-in-law as well as chairman of the Chase National Bank,” spoke at the Bohemian Club with Lawrence on May 13, 1940** (p. 316) [IVORY: Eastern financiers]. - Off-topic within ch7: pp. 286–288 (Greek revival pageantry), 311–314 and 316–320 (general Manhattan Project narrative). Read in full.

## Ivory crossovers (Yale / East Coast beats)
- **Daniel Coit Gilman:** UC president 1872–75, “fresh from Yale’s Sheffield Scientific School” (p. 282). Web-verified: Yale 1852 and Skull and Bones; he incorporated its Russell Trust in 1856. He then left for Johns Hopkins.
- **William H. Crocker:** “graduated from Yale’s Sheffield Scientific School in 1882” (p. 258). Web-verified: Book and Snake, not Bones. He presided over the Pacific Improvement Co., headed the state Republican Party, dominated the UC regents, sat on the PG&E board 1905–37 and funded Lawrence. Charles F. Crocker (his brother) was a named Stanford founding trustee.
- **John Hays Hammond** (Sheffield 1876, Book and Snake, web-verified): his “college classmate, Walker Blaine,” opened the door to Secretary of State Blaine for Irving Scott’s *Oregon* contract (p. 128). Hammond’s word only (fixes §27).
- **Francis G. Newlands:** “Yale-educated.” Sharon heir by marriage, he laid out Burlingame and Hillsborough and sponsored the Reclamation Act after buying the land (ch2 n25–26). Hall McAllister Jr., his law partner, was the nephew of Ward McAllister, who invented NY’s “Four Hundred” (ch2 n15).
- **Ernest Lawrence:** arrived Aug. 1928 “fresh from Yale” (p. 307; LBL confirms).
- **William H. Taft** (Yale 1878, Skull and Bones): Bernard Moses was his “friend and publicist” on the Philippine Commission (n27). Barrows was a Taft appointee (p. 300).
- **Rockefeller / Chase:** Rockefeller Foundation >$1M for the 184-inch cyclotron. **Winthrop Aldrich**, chairman of Chase National Bank and a Rockefeller Foundation board member, spoke at the Bohemian Club luncheon with Lawrence on May 13, 1940 (p. 316). Brechin calls him “John D. Rockefeller’s son-in-law”; he was actually the brother of Abby Aldrich Rockefeller, so the **brother-in-law of John D. Rockefeller Jr.** (do-not-import, fixes). Hearst Oil was in the Mills Buildings and partnered with the Mills family (ch6 n20). Cerro de Pasco was backed by Morgan, Vanderbilt, Frick and Mills (ch5).

Schwab/Bethlehem bought Union Iron Works. Kuhn, Loeb sold Japan’s war bonds (ch3 n59). A Vanderbilt-led NY syndicate built Philippine railroads (p. 140).
- **Hearst:** educated at St. Paul’s and Harvard; Wall Street used the NY *Herald* against him in 1906 (ch5 n37).
- **Bohemian Grove** as the East–West switchboard: Hoover, Warren, McLaughlin and the Sept. 1942 Manhattan Project meeting (p. 318).
- **E. H. Harriman** appears twice: in the San Fernando/Owens Valley syndicate with Huntington and Otis (p. 105), and in the graft probe, where “even E.H. Harriman, head of the Southern Pacific system, were named” (ch4). *Not in Brechin:* Dulles, Skull and Bones by name, and Delano, which appears only as FDR’s middle name (verified by full-text search).

# Cardinal close reading – Chang, Ghosts of Gold Mountain

**Citation scheme:** print page from HMH 2019 ebook page anchors [[p. N]] + ¶ within chapter; keyword notes keyed in.

**Book:** Gordon H. Chang, *Ghosts of Gold Mountain: The Epic Story of the Chinese Who Built the Transcontinental Railroad* (Boston: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, 2019). Ebook ISBN 9781328618610; hardcover 9781328618573. Cardinal Drive.

**Clean extract.** Publisher HMH ebook (clean XHTML, not OCR). Working text extracted locally for search (not published). The ebook carries **print page anchors**, rendered [[p. N]], so we **cite print pages** plus ¶ within each chapter. Notes are unnumbered keyword notes (“*Keyword:* source”) linked to anchors. the local keyed file gives each note with the text page it annotates; we cite them as “n. to p. N (‘keyword’).”

**Method.** Chapters were read paragraph by paragraph, except where a chapter is flagged off-topic (keyword-scanned, with relevant paragraphs read in full). Yale/East Coast crossovers are tagged **[IVORY]** and gathered at the end.

**Author context (conflict note).** Chang is a Stanford history professor. The book grew out of the **Stanford-based Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project**, which he “helped establish and then co-direct” (p. 9 ¶23). Stanford’s railroad-fortune origin is the subject of his book, so watch how he treats Stanford himself.

---


## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 — Intro, chs 1–10, Conclusion, Acknowledgments (pp. 1–248), all relevant keyword notes. Read in full: Intro, chs 2, 3, 7, 10, Conclusion, Acks. Read by…

## Introduction (pp. 1–13): read in full
- pp. 1–5: Promontory, May 10, 1869. Strobridge (the CPRR construction boss) hosted headman Hung Wah and other Chinese in his car. The Chinese had not been invited to the ceremony, Russell’s photo, “or join the elite reception in the train car of Leland Stanford, the CPRR president” (p. 5 ¶10). The headline was “Chinese Laborers at Table.”
- **p. 2–3 ¶5: “Upwards of twenty thousand Chinese, 90 percent of the CPRR construction labor force.”** CPRR 690 miles vs UP 1,086.
- p. 3 ¶6: the Golden Spike engraving, “May God continue the unity of our Country …” (the note cites a 2013 Stanford news release; the spike is at Stanford’s Cantor Arts Center).
- p. 4 ¶7: Strobridge had opposed hiring Chinese and argued with Charles Crocker, one of the “Big Four” with Stanford, Huntington and Hopkins.
- p. 4 ¶8: Hung Wah started with the CPRR in Jan. 1864; he was an Auburn figure and headman over hundreds or thousands.
- p. 6 ¶16: in 1969 Volpe: “Who else but Americans could drill tunnels …”
- p. 7 ¶18: 1864–69 the Chinese were “by far the largest single workforce in American industry to that date.” Rev. John Todd: “The road could never have been built without the Chinamen.”
- p. 8 ¶20: no text by any Railroad Chinese worker has ever been found. PMSC carried >250,000 letters in 1876.
- **p. 9 ¶23 (STANFORD):** the research base is the Stanford project Chang co-directed for six years.
- p. 12 ¶31: questions on the 1867 strike (“three thousand Chinese”) and the death toll.

## Ch. 1 “Guangdong” (pp. 14–37): OFF-TOPIC for Cardinal, with the relevant paragraphs read in full
- Why off-topic: Siyi geography, village life, folk religion, clan feuds, Huie Kin’s migration memoir and the voyage. None of it touches Stanford, land, money or state power except the items below. Keyword-scanned for Stanford/Crocker/Huntington/PMSC/coolie/Yale/New York etc.
- **p. 28 ¶41 (railroad money in migration):** PMSC “and, later, the Occidental and Oriental Steamship Company, formed directly by railroad companies, profited handsomely from the travel.” More than 112,000 Chinese left Hong Kong for the US in 1860–74. [Cardinal: O&O was CP/UP-owned (1874). Verify.]
- p. 25 ¶32 [IVORY]: Yung Wing, “1854 Yale graduate,” saw the Guangzhou executions.
- pp. 33–36 ¶62–68: the coolie trade (500,000 Chinese to Peru and Cuba; 12% death rate on American ships). Minister John Ward: “a disgrace … upon our flag.” **Congress in 1862 outlawed Americans and American ships from the coolie trade**, and the Hong Kong consulate certified “free and voluntary” emigration. Chang: no firm evidence that Chinese entering the US were indentured. The credit-ticket system, he says, was mischaracterized as servility “largely emanated from racial prejudice” (p. 31 ¶58).

## Ch. 2 “Gold Mountain” (pp. 38–54): read in full
- Cardinal relevance: low to moderate. Legal exclusion, the “free labor” vs. coerced-labor dispute (this bears on how the CPRR got its labor), and Six Companies.
- p. 39 ¶4: the Nationality Act of 1790 limited naturalization to “free, white persons”; the 1866 Act and Fourteenth Amendment left Chinese out.
- p. 39–40 ¶6: PMSC’s *Great Republic* (1867–79) carried ~10,000 Chinese. In Nov. 1869 it brought ~1,300, “many likely coming for railroad work.”
- p. 43 ¶13: about 500 of 58,000 gold seekers in 1850 were Chinese. From 1852 to the early 1860s, 6,000–7,000 arrived a year.
- p. 44 ¶14: *Alta*, 1854: Chinese would do the work white men would “never” do. “Roads have to be made, and railroads will soon follow.”
- pp. 44–45 ¶15–16: the 1876 federal commission could not agree on numbers (67,000 to 210,000+).
- **p. 45 ¶18 (CPRR labor):** the *NY Evening Post* (1869): “nearly the whole force which built the Central Pacific railroad were brought over as free laborers.” They came under consul-approved contracts arranged by an unidentified American businessman working with Chinese merchants: passage was advanced, a deposit covered return of remains, and wages paid off the advance (some mortgaged real property). [IVORY-adjacent: an East Coast paper as character witness.]
- pp. 46–48 ¶20–25: Six Companies (huiguan). Leung Cook testified to the 1876 state commission (Ning Yeung: $5 exit fee; repatriation of remains).
- pp. 48–52 ¶27–32: photographers Carleton Watkins and Lai Yong. Lai Yong’s 1873 “The Chinese Question from a Chinese Standpoint”: Chinese had “toiled patiently to build your railroads.”
- **pp. 52–54 ¶34–37 (coercion counter-evidence; CPRR):** attorney Daniel Cleveland’s unpublished manuscript (late 1868 or early 1869; his report reached Seward). Credit-ticket arrivals “are taken possession of by their white owners, and are treated like slaves, watched and guarded, until they reach the end of their journey, and are delivered to the Railroad Company.” Men with bludgeons guarded them on the tug. They were shipped upriver to Sacramento and **locked in railroad boxcars**; some jumped and died. **This conflicts with Chang’s own “came freely” framing (¶18–19) and with the CPRR’s later testimony. Chang presents both without reconciling them.** It is a key item for Cardinal on CPRR labor procurement.

## Ch. 3 “Central Pacific” (pp. 55–74): read in full. CORE (Stanford, the Big Four, labor procurement, federal subsidy)
- p. 55 ¶2: by summer 1868, 10,000 Railroad Chinese made up 90% of the force.
- **p. 56 ¶4 (STANFORD; IVORY):** Asa Whitney (NY merchant, China trade) promoted the Pacific road: “Through us must be the route to Asia.” **“Among those who shared the vision was a young Leland Stanford in upstate New York, who listened as Whitney sought to persuade Leland’s father to join his crusade”** (n. to p. 56: “Biographical Sketch,” *Memorial Addresses on … Leland Stanford*, Senate, 53rd Cong., 2nd sess., 1894, 11; a hagiographic source).
- pp. 56–57 ¶5–6: Sen. Benton imagined Chinese labor and intermarriage: “Commerce is a great civilizer.” Speer’s *The Oriental* (1855) predicted “Chinese builders of iron roads.”
- p. 57–58 ¶8 [IVORY]: the “New York−based Panama Railway Company” brought 1,000 Chinese to Panama in 1854, and 50% died.
- p. 58 ¶9: in 1858 the California Central hired 50 Chinese, and Chinese worked on the San Jose–San Francisco line.
- p. 58–59 ¶10–13: Zhigang of the Burlingame delegation [IVORY: Anson Burlingame, Massachusetts/Harvard] rode a train on Apr. 16, 1868.
- p. 59–61 ¶14–35: Gov. McDougal praised the Chinese (1852); Gov. Bigler sought a Foreign Miners’ Tax and head tax (1852) and later sympathized with the Confederacy. **n. to p. 61: Bigler was “later in his career … appointed a federal commissioner to oversee the construction of the Pacific railroad”** (state-power crossover). Norman Asing: “aristocracy of skin.”
- **p. 61 ¶37 (STANFORD; key quote):** in his 1862 gubernatorial (inaugural) address, Stanford said: “The settlement among us of an inferior race is to be discouraged”; “Asia, with her numberless millions, sends to our shores the dregs of her population”; the Chinese are “a degraded and distinct people” exercising “a deleterious influence upon the superior race.” It drew warm applause and remains “his best-known comments on the Chinese.” (n. to p. 62: governors.library.ca.gov; Chang’s own essay “The Chinese and the Stanfords,” in Chang & Fishkin eds., *Chinese and the Iron Road*, Stanford UP 2019; Julie Cain M.A. thesis, 2011.)
- **pp. 61–63 ¶38–40 (STANFORD; Chang’s defense):** his sentiments were “apparently politically motivated.” In private the Stanfords kept Chinese servants: cook Moy Jin Kee and his brother Moy Jin Mun, whom Jane reportedly proposed to adopt and gave an engraved gold ring (family history). In 1862 Chinese herbalist Yee Fung Cheung treated Jane’s pulmonary illness. **“Stanford himself, as the president of the CPRR, … would be responsible for attracting more Chinese to America than any other single individual.”** He “directly employed hundreds of Chinese on his many private and commercial properties … including at his stock farm in Palo Alto.” “At the end of his life, Stanford rued his earlier prejudice.” **They “had, of course, helped him become one of the richest men in the world.”** All of ¶38–40 is sourced “Ibid.” to Chang’s own essay and the Cain thesis. **Caution: this is a Stanford-affiliated author’s mitigation, and the “rued” claim needs its primary (Stanford’s 1887 Pacific Railway Commission testimony?).**
- **p. 63–64 ¶42 (federal subsidy):** Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act (July 1862): land grants, bonds and loans; competition “encouraged financial malfeasance, slipshod work, political intrigue, bribery, and industrial sabotage.” **“Eventually, the two railroad companies obtained more than 175 million square miles of public land in subsidies”: an ERROR (impossible; the whole US is ~3.8M sq mi).** Crédit Mobilier. (n. cites Bain and White, *Railroaded*.)
- p. 64 ¶44: the *Sacramento Union* (Oct. 14, 1865) said the line needed 50,000 tons of iron and 1.1M ties. The CPRR started at “Colfax, fifty-five miles north of Sacramento, where the line actually began” (odd phrasing; the line began at Sacramento).
- **p. 66 ¶48 (STANFORD; dates):** Stanford broke ground in Jan. 1863. **“Assuming office in 1861, Stanford had lobbied vigorously for federal government support.”** [Check: he was elected Sept. 1861 and inaugurated Jan. 10, 1862.] The Big Four established the CPRR in June 1861 “anticipating the federal government’s decision.” They were thought “a little off,” even “insane” (n. to p. 67: Alfred E. Davis testimony, PRC vol. 6, 3620–26).
- p. 67 ¶49–50: the leaders “because of their racial prejudice … initially wanted only whites.” Clement: “It was impossible to get white labor.” From Jan. 1863 to June 1864 the line reached only Newcastle (31 mi). They considered Confederate prisoners, freedmen and Mexicans (n.: Saxton; Oscar Lewis, *Big Four*).
- p. 67–68 ¶51–52: Crocker’s manservant Ah Ling may have suggested Chinese labor (conjecture by Crocker descendants; Chang’s 2016 conversation). Strobridge: “I will not boss Chinese.” Crocker: “Did they not build the Chinese wall …?” (PRC vol. 7, 3660.)
- pp. 68–72 ¶53–66: Hung Wah, Auburn labor contractor (b. 1831/35, d. 1931). In 1862 he contracted 150 workers for 60% of the gold dust (*Roush v. Terry*). Aug. 1863 ad: “I will furnish any number of Chinese laborers to work on Rail Roads.” *People v. Hall* (1854) barred Chinese testimony. Cleveland to J. Ross Browne, July 21, 1868 (forwarded to Seward).
- **p. 72 ¶67 (CPRR):** the Jan. 1864 CPRR payroll is the first firm evidence of Chinese workers: Hung Wah signed for ~$675. Crocker: “50 Chinamen” then “50 more.” They were put to work “on what was known as the **Dutch Flat–Donner Lake Wagon Road**, which the CPRR would use for access.” [Cardinal: the wagon road was the Big Four’s privately owned toll road (the “Dutch Flat swindle”). Chang omits that ownership; cross-check with White.]
- **p. 73 ¶68–69 (wages):** by spring 1865, 2,000–3,000 Chinese and 800 whites. Chinese were paid ~$26/month and paid their own room and board; whites got “perhaps 30 percent more” (n.: *Sacramento Union*, May 1, 1865; Crocker PRC 7:3659–60).

## Ch. 4 “Foothills” (pp. 75–97): construction narrative, read by keyword-plus-lead scan with every relevant paragraph read in full
- Lower-value material, scanned: scenery and environment (pp. 75–77), Curry’s diary of hardship (pp. 77–80), the photo-technique discussion (pp. 93–97).
- pp. 77–80 ¶9–15: engineer Stephen Allen Curry (a Union veteran from New York) was hired by Stanford, Montague and Clement (Dec. 1864). His diary records Cape Horn at a 70° slope, snow in April, and “What a home for white men.” He quit in June 1865.
- **pp. 82–84 ¶20–37 (insider construction payrolls):** “the payroll sheets of **construction companies affiliated with the CPRR**” are the only personnel records. [Cardinal: these are the Big Four’s insider construction firms (Charles Crocker & Co.; later the Contract and Finance Co.; cf. White, CANON-059). Chang doesn’t name or analyze them.] Payroll #128 (Apr. 1865) lists contractors including “Sisson’s,” “the largest labor contracting company” [Sisson, Wallace & Co.; check the Crocker family tie]. Up to 500 Chinese contractors supplied perhaps half of the 5,000–6,000 Chinese in the early years.
- **p. 84 ¶39:** Hung Wah had 500+ men by Apr. 1866 and 900+ by July 1866, “almost one quarter of the total construction workforce.” That July he received ~$28,000 (“$784,000” today).
- **p. 85 ¶42 (STATE POWER):** E. B. Crocker (Charles’s brother, retired CA Supreme Court justice, CPRR attorney), Apr. 1865 letter: Chinese “prove nearly equal to white men … far more reliable”; “no danger of strikes among them.” The letter went to Senator **Cornelius Cole** (n. to p. 85: Phillips, *Cornelius Cole*, 138). A company lawyer was briefing a sitting U.S. senator.
- **pp. 85–86 ¶43–45 (STANFORD; key quotes):** Stanford to stockholders (July 13, 1865): Chinese are “an important element of labor.” **Stanford’s Oct. 10, 1865 *Statement Made to the President of the United States, and Secretary of the Interior*** (required by Congress because public money was involved): “They are quiet, peaceable, patient, industrious and economical”; “more prudent and economical” and “**contented with less wages**”; “No system similar to slavery, serfdom or peonage prevails among these laborers”; wages “always paid in coin each month.” He predicted 15,000 Chinese the next year. (The pamphlet was printed by H. S. Crocker & Co., another Crocker brother’s firm; n. to p. 86.) **This is a direct contrast with his 1862 inaugural address.**
- p. 86 ¶46: rock excavations expected to take 18 months took 4–5 (Stanford, Miller, Montague to the directors, Jan. 5, 1867, PRC vol. 5, 3050–51).
- **pp. 87–92 ¶47–63 (the Cape Horn baskets):**
  - Debunkers (Edson T. Strobridge, 2001) say an SP publicist invented the basket story in 1927.
  - Chang cites pre-1927 sources: Crofutt’s guide (1869), Nelson’s guide (1870), Isabella Bird (1873), and the *Pittsfield Eagle* (1868), reprinted in seven Eastern papers: “let down in baskets … 460 of these charges.”
  - Montague (Oct. 8, 1864) put the slope at ~75°.
  - **The claim that 300+ Chinese died at Cape Horn has “Firm evidence … yet to be found.”**
  - His conclusion: the baskets “cannot be dismissed as myth.”
- **pp. 92–94 ¶64–66 (IVORY; finance):** photographer Alfred Hart (from Connecticut) shot Jane Stanford boating on Donner Lake and Stanford at Promontory. **E. B. Crocker to Huntington (Jan. 9, 1867): Hart’s images were “universally admired”; “The company sent many of them to Huntington for his use in raising capital”** in New York. Hart’s photos are now in Stanford’s Green Library Special Collections (n.).
- p. 97 ¶75: Bloomer Cut.

## Ch. 5 “The High Sierra” (pp. 98–120): read by keyword-plus-lead scan, with relevant paragraphs in full
- Lower-value material, scanned: night sky and festival calendar (pp. 98–100), archaeology of camps (pp. 102–106), diet, fishing and farming (pp. 108–113), religion and the Hungry Ghost festival (pp. 116–120). The scan flagged no Stanford, money or power content in these passages.
- **p. 100 ¶7 (STATE POWER; IVORY):** in Aug. 1865 Stanford hosted Speaker **Schuyler Colfax**, other dignitaries “and prominent eastern journalists” on the line: an effort “of great magnitude and National importance.” The force was 4,000, about 90% Chinese and 10% Irish. p. 109–110 ¶27: the Six Companies gave Colfax a six-hour, 336-dish “state banquet” at the Hang Heong. (Cardinal: Colfax was later implicated in Crédit Mobilier.)
- p. 100 ¶8: engineer George E. Gray’s report says the work would “compare most favorably … with any railroad in the United States.” It was printed by H. S. Crocker, with a Stanford letter.
- p. 101 ¶8: “Getting past the summit … was essential if the company was to control the critical rail traffic between Nevada and California and survive financially.”
- **pp. 106–107 ¶22 (deaths; company policy):** Chief engineer Clement said tunnel work had to continue through winter “no matter what the cost.” Strobridge: “In many instances our camps were carried away by snowslides … Men were buried and many of them were not found until the snow melted.” Bodies were found standing, “still holding their shovels.” **Source: Clement to Stanford (July 21, 1887) and Strobridge to Stanford (July 23, 1887), reproduced in PRC vol. 5, 2576–78**: letters solicited by Stanford for the Pacific Railway Commission.
- p. 103 ¶15: “the railroad company never wanted to keep more workers on the payroll than necessary”; workers were released in deep winter.
- **p. 114 ¶40 (MONEY; insider self-dealing):** Sisson, Wallace & Co., founded 1857 as a merchandising and Chinese import firm, was “the largest contracting company for the CPRR.” From 1866 it recruited workers in China, with offices in Hong Kong, SF and Truckee. It took little for contracting but “required that it control provisioning.” Profits came from tools, clothes, liquor, opium and food. **“The arrangement was lucrative, especially for the Crocker family, which benefited at each level of the operation. Charles Crocker, a director of the CPRR, also headed its main construction company, Crocker Construction. As a boss of one company, he therefore essentially paid himself as the head of the other.”** **Clark W. Crocker** was a chief partner of Sisson, Wallace (n. to p. 114: renamed Sisson, Crocker & Co.; *Wallace v. Sisson*, June 9, 1893, *California Unreported Cases* vol. 4, 34–47). This is the strongest money item in the chapter; cross-ref White CANON-059.
- p. 113–115 ¶39–41: contractors made their money on provisioning rather than wage cuts. Ah Louis’s records are at Stanford’s Green Library.

## Ch. 6 “The Summit” (pp. 121–137): read by keyword-plus-lead scan, with relevant paragraphs in full
- Lower-value material, scanned: tunnel engineering, Hart photo analysis and snowsheds (pp. 125–137).
- p. 121–122 ¶2–5: on July 4, 1866, Chinese workers rode in the CPRR parade in Sacramento. Crocker: “the iron horse was now puffing his nostrils at an altitude of over 3,600 feet.” Six Companies: about a quarter of California’s 58,000 Chinese worked for the CPRR or on “other public improvements.”
- p. 122–123 ¶6: the line reached Dutch Flat (mile 67) and then Cisco (mile 92, Nov. 1866). The company ran 100 locomotives.
- **pp. 123–124 ¶8–9 (STANFORD):** in his 1866 report, Stanford called the work “the most difficult ever yet surmounted by any railroad in the United States, if not in Europe … a herculean task.” He said it was costly because the company had to pay in gold for “all labor.” It wanted 15,000 workers but got 10,000, kept 6,000 through winter, and planned 20,000. The California Powder Works near Santa Cruz (opened 1864) had 275 workers, all Chinese.
- p. 125 ¶11: a five-mile single tunnel was considered (~$1M a mile).
- **p. 127 ¶17 (IVORY: New York):** in the winter of 1866–67 there were 44 storms. E. B. Crocker reminded “an impatient Collis Huntington in New York” that the summit “is a rough place in a storm.”
- **p. 136 ¶32:** nitroglycerine was made on site near Donner Lake, and an April 1866 explosion killed six workers. The company dropped it “not because of its danger but because of patent restrictions … Alfred Nobel, and government restrictions.”

## Ch. 7 “The Strike” (pp. 138–165): read in full, paragraph by paragraph
The main sources are the Crocker, Hopkins and Huntington letters (Huntington Papers microfilm), plus 1876 Senate testimony and 1887 PRC testimony.
- **p. 138 ¶2 (IVORY: New York capital):** in Jan. 1867, E. B. Crocker wrote to Huntington, “ensconced in New York City raising capital for the railroad project”: shrinking the force “can’t be done … it will be fatal.” (n.: E. B. Crocker to Huntington, Jan. 10 and 31, 1867.)
- **p. 139–140 ¶4 (STANFORD):** Stanford, E. H. Miller Jr. and S. S. Montague reported to the board on Jan. 5, 1867, asking for a “large force, probably twenty thousand” (PRC vol. 5, 3050–51). The company had 5,000 Chinese-language handbills printed to circulate “all over this state & in China.” No copy survives.
- **p. 140 ¶5 (MONEY / lifestyle):** “The top officers of the company assumed high financial risk and eventually became enormously wealthy.” Huntington lived at New York’s Metropolitan Hotel and then a Park Avenue mansion. **Stanford “had his own mansion in Sacramento, which he acquired when he was governor.”** Strobridge’s camp train housed about 500 mostly white workers.
- **p. 141–142 ¶8:** Chinese tunnelers outperformed Cornish miners (Crocker’s Senate testimony, Nov. 14, 1876, pp. 666–88).
- **p. 142 ¶9:** the Nov. 1866 payroll for Summit camp 51 “A” lists Chinese waiters at $0.66 a day, Chinese construction workers at $1 a day and white blacksmiths at $2.50 a day with no board deducted. (CSRM MS 79.)
- p. 143 ¶10: Clement on Chinese workers: “never took any particular interest in them, never cared about them so long as we got the work done” (PRC 6:3217).
- p. 143–144 ¶12–13: wages. White carpenters got $4 a day with board. Clement: white woodcutters $40 a month with board, Chinese $30 without. Gilliss: Chinese at the Summit Tunnel $31 a month without board; white foremen $120 with board.
- **p. 144–145 ¶14–16 (MONEY: admission under oath):** in Senate testimony, Crocker said Chinese were paid $35 a month and spent about 40¢ a day at the company store. Strobridge: “sometimes we did not pay for two months and perhaps more”; Chinese labor was “much cheaper. Their board is an important consideration.” Asked, **“Did you make more money out of [employing Chinese] than if you had employed white men?” Crocker: “I think I did.”** (*Report of the Joint Special Committee to Investigate Chinese Immigration*, 44th Cong. 2d sess., 1877, 671–88, 723–28.)
- p. 147 ¶22: Chinese insisted on pay in gold coin, unlike UP workers, who were paid in paper. Where the money went is unknown (“ghost money”).
- **p. 147–148 ¶23–26:** the strike of June 1867 was “the largest, or certainly close to it, workers’ strike against a private employer … to that date.” Chang argues that “it was the company’s vulnerability, not desperation among the Chinese,” that drove it. “The company was in shaky financial condition.”
- p. 149 ¶29: on May 16, 1867, E. B. Crocker wrote that “Several of our largest Capitalists” had toured the line. **“The cheapness is due in a great measure to the low price of Chinese labor.”**
- p. 149 ¶30: other employers were now hiring Chinese: “Our use of them has led hundreds of others to employ them.”
- **p. 150 ¶31 (STANFORD; Sisson link):** Stanford to Hopkins, May 18, 1867: Stanford had learned from a friend and from his “own personal Chinese contacts” of widespread unhappiness among Chinese workers contracted under “Sisson.” (Ties to ch. 5 ¶40 on Crocker family self-dealing.)
- p. 150 ¶32: the company raised Chinese wages from $31 to $35 a month in May 1867. Hopkins: work was “impossible” without the Chinese.
- **p. 151 ¶33 (STATE POWER):** “Desperate, the company appealed to the federal government to send ‘5,000 negroes to work building the road.’” (n.: E. B. Crocker to Huntington, June 4, 1867; Hopkins to Huntington, June 26, 1867.) **Needs verification:** which federal body (the Freedmen’s Bureau?) and whether there is a primary document. Chang’s note cites only private letters.
- p. 151 ¶34: a tunnel explosion near Cisco on June 19 killed a white man named Burns and “five Chinamen.”
- **pp. 151–152 ¶35–39:** on June 24, 1867, 3,000 Chinese struck from Cisco to Truckee. Demands: $40 a month (parity), a 10-hour day (some reports said 8), shorter tunnel shifts. The *Sacramento Daily Union* reported a protest against overseers’ “right … to either whip them or restrain them from leaving the road.” Chang notes this is uncorroborated.
- **p. 153–154 ¶40–42:** Strobridge’s wire: “chinamen have all struck for $40 & time to be reduced from 11 to 10 hours.” Hopkins: if they succeed, “they control.” E. B. Crocker, June 27: “they are getting smart … we would always be in their power. The only safe way for us is to inundate this state and Nevada with laborers, Freedmen, Chinese, Japanese.” Charles Crocker: “John Chinaman no make laws for me; I make laws for Chinaman.” **Hopkins: “A Negro labor force will tend to keep the chinese steady, as the chinese have kept the Irishmen quiet.”** He asked Huntington to send workers “from the East.” [IVORY]
- **p. 155–156 ¶44 (STATE POWER / coercion):** the strike was ended by cutting off provisions. E. B. Crocker credited the Chinese agents; Charles Crocker claimed he cut them off himself. “None of us went near them for a week … We did not want to exhibit anxiety.” Strikers were told to return or forfeit all June pay. Crocker’s security force would “shoot down any man”; **“the local sheriff and armed guards”** were on hand. (Cardinal: county police power deployed for the company.)
- p. 156 ¶45: Hopkins blamed “chinese gamblers and opium traders.” Charles Crocker suspected UP agents.
- **p. 156–157 ¶46:** “The CPRR, highly dependent on public funding and private investments,” needed to appear in control for investors.
- p. 157 ¶47: after the strike, pay quietly rose above $35 for skilled Chinese workers, from $26 in 1864.
- **p. 158 ¶51 (STATE POWER):** E. B. Crocker showed visiting Washington officials the work. A federal inspector, “a Mr. Johnson,” was “highly pleased,” and “his report to the Secretary of the Interior will be all that we can ask.” (n.: E. B. Crocker to Huntington, July 23, 1867.) Cardinal: the company’s confidence about the government inspector’s report.
- **p. 159 ¶53 (SMOKING-GUN class quote):** E. B. Crocker, Sept. 12, 1867: **“We want 100,000 chinamen here so as to bring the price of labor down.”** Huntington, Oct. 3, 1867: **“I like the idea of your getting over more Chinamen; it would be all the better for us and the state if then should a half million come over in 1868.”** The company worked with steamship companies on “favorable arrangements.” California’s 1860 population was under 400,000.
- p. 159–160 ¶54: later strikes. Stockton, 1869. The Santa Cruz Mountains (1870s), where a thousand Chinese built rail and timber lines. Tehachapi, 1875, 3,000 strikers.
- p. 161 ¶57: E. B. Crocker to Huntington, Aug. 10, 1867, describing seam blasts.
- p. 162 ¶59–61: snowsheds: 37 miles and 65 million feet of timber. Arthur Brown called the expense “appalling and unprecedented” (Brown to Stanford, July 25, 1887, PRC 5:2581).
- p. 163–164 ¶64: Gilliss: a slide at Tunnel No. 10 killed “fifteen or twenty Railroad Chinese.”
- p. 164 ¶66: Hopkins said Chinese at the summit went “blind” from snow glare. E. B. Crocker: “we have had to buy up all the cheap goggles in the market.”

## Ch. 8 “Truckee” (pp. 165–188): read by scan
Leads of every paragraph were read; relevant paragraphs were read in full. **Largely off-topic for Cardinal:** Truckee social history, gambling, food, prostitution (¶37–48), marriage and remittances, and folk songs (¶49–121). Nothing on Stanford, land or state power except:
- p. 168 ¶14: Ling Sing murder (1854), Nevada County violence.
- **p. 173 ¶26 (MONEY; contractors):** white-owned contractors “like Egbert, Booth and, most important, Sisson, Wallace” were taking over “the lucrative contracting business.” **In June 1866 Sisson received almost $61,000 (about 2,000 workers).** SF businessman **Cornelius Koopmanschap** was “perhaps the largest individual labor contractor,” bringing “hundreds, and possibly thousands” to the CPRR. (Combine with ch. 5 ¶40: Clark W. Crocker was a partner of Sisson.)
- p. 173 ¶27: Governor Frederick Low contributed $500 to the reward in the McDaniel murder (Auburn, Jan. 1867).
- p. 171 ¶20: a baby named “Colfax Ah,” likely after Vice President Colfax, who passed through Truckee in Oct. 1869.
- p. 178 ¶41: the decline of Chinese prostitution is attributed partly to federal legislation targeting Chinese women (the Page Act, 1875, implied).
- p. 175 ¶37: SF police managed the arrival of nearly 400 Chinese women on the steamer *China* in March 1869 (Pacific Mail).

## Ch. 9 “The Golden Spike” (pp. 188–207): read by scan
Leads of every paragraph were read and keyword paragraphs read in full. The rest is construction narrative (Nevada canyons, ten-mile day mechanics, Russell photo analysis).
- **p. 189 ¶5 (LAND):** the meeting point was aimed north of Salt Lake, “where the land granted by the federal government to the Central Pacific and Union Pacific was most agreeable.” Both companies bickered “until almost the last moment.”
- **p. 195 ¶19:** Charles Crocker, fall 1868: 10,000 Chinese, 1,000 whites, “any number” of Native Americans. “No list of names was kept.” His “scheme of employing, working and paying them by the wholesale” meant workers were paid through overseers, avoiding “lengthy bookkeeping.” Crocker: “Indians and Chinese were so much alike personally that no human being could tell them apart.” (Cardinal: anonymity was a company accounting choice.)
- p. 197–198 ¶24–26: Irish (UP) vs. Chinese blasting skirmishes. Durant bet Crocker on the ten-mile day.
- p. 199 ¶29–30: the ten-mile day (Apr. 28, 1869). A U.S. Army officer: “a good day’s march for an army.” Eight Irish rail handlers are named; no Chinese are.
- **p. 200 ¶31:** “Promontory Summit, where Congress on April 9, 1869, determined the two lines would meet.” **Check:** the Huntington–Dodge agreement was Apr. 9, 1869; the congressional joint resolution was approved Apr. 10, 1869. Chang conflates them (minor).
- **p. 201–202 ¶35–37 (STANFORD):** Stanford “occupied the center of the event” but gave a “forgettable, less than three-minute-long speech.” No speaker mentioned the workers. **“The Golden Spike sits in the art museum at Stanford University.”** The laurel tie was destroyed in 1906. Stanford hosted a party in his parlor car and left at 2:00.
- p. 203 ¶39: E. B. Crocker, Sacramento, May 8, 1869: completion was “in large measure due to that poor, despised class of laborers called the Chinese.” Charles Crocker praised Chinese “as a working class” when welcoming Vice President Colfax.
- p. 203 ¶40: of the CPRR leaders, “only Leland Stanford made it to the ceremony.” Huntington, Hopkins and both Crockers were absent.
- p. 204 ¶41 [IVORY]: eastern celebrations, including Philadelphia’s Liberty Bell.
- p. 204 ¶43: Stanford’s special train hit a log past Truckee.
- **p. 205 ¶44 (contrast):** UP workers held Durant hostage for back wages. Durant “had to wire for $800,000” and was released on May 8. Chang: the UP had “engaged in financial mismanagement.” [IVORY: Durant / UP / Crédit Mobilier]
- p. 205–206 ¶45: Rev. John Todd (Massachusetts) gave the benediction: “China is our neighbor now.” [IVORY]

## Ch. 10 “Beyond Promontory” (pp. 209–236): read in full, paragraph by paragraph
- p. 210 ¶2: “California-grown strawberries could go east, as they did with Stanford for his banquet at Promontory.”
- p. 210 ¶4 [IVORY]: the article “The Chinaman as a Railroad Builder” ran in 20+ papers, including the *National Intelligencer* and the New York–based *Scientific American*.
- p. 212–213 ¶9–11: post-Promontory dispersal. The legend that workers were abandoned in the desert is disputed by Chang (Ng Poon Chew: jobs “were not wanting at all”). **Koopmanschap**, “who had made a name for himself providing Chinese to the CPRR,” told the July 1869 Memphis convention he could “meet all the demands of the South.” [IVORY / Eastern & Southern capital]
- p. 213 ¶10 [IVORY]: the *New York Commercial Advertiser* reported Charleston planters wanted 50,000 Chinese.
- **p. 214 ¶14 (Big Four expansion):** “the Central Pacific line … down the San Joaquin Valley toward Los Angeles”: Tehachapi (17 tunnels), the San Fernando Tunnel (~7,000 ft), and the SP to Arizona and Texas, built by thousands of Chinese. The Northern Pacific was the largest employer (6,000+). [IVORY: the NP was Jay Cooke-financed, though Chang doesn’t name him]
- p. 215 ¶17: immigration from 1869 to 1877 averaged 15,000 a year (20,000+ in 1873), “far lower than the grand numbers that were tossed around by the Big Four.”
- p. 215 ¶18 [IVORY]: New York had 300 Chinese laundries by 1879.
- p. 217 ¶21 [IVORY]: the New York *Merchants’ Magazine and Commercial Review* (Aug. 1869) on the “Coming Chinese.”
- p. 218 ¶22 [IVORY]: *Frank Leslie’s* series “The Coming Man” (Thomas W. Knox, 1870).
- p. 218 ¶23: Charles Crocker: “are men, good and true men.” Chang: “sincere respect for those who had made him very wealthy.”
- **p. 219 ¶24 (STATE POWER; IVORY):** the Burlingame Treaty (1868). Anson Burlingame was Lincoln’s minister to China and then China’s envoy. The treaty guaranteed free immigration. Cardinal: the treaty secured the CPRR’s labor pipeline.
- p. 219–220 ¶26: the 1870 Naturalization Act extended naturalization to people of African descent, but not Chinese. Chinese were barred until 1943.
- p. 220 ¶27: in 1868, SF Chinese leaders set aside $10,000 to repatriate about 300 bodies.
- **p. 221 ¶29 [IVORY]:** “Famed New York jurist and future U.S. attorney general **Edwards Pierrepont**” said at the **New York banquet for Burlingame’s Chinese embassy, June 23, 1868**, that shippers “take out dead Chinamen” and “bring back live ones.” (Pierrepont: Yale 1837. Web-verify if used.)
- p. 222 ¶32: in spring 1868, a gang identified as KKK lynched four Chinese at Grass Valley.
- **p. 222 ¶34:** “the company kept no records of personnel killed on the job.” The Lake Tahoe drowning legend (800 men) has “no evidence.”
- **pp. 222–223 ¶35:** Clement: “many laborers lost their lives.” Strobridge: men buried until spring (these quotes come from **1887 letters to Stanford** for the PRC; see ch. 5). Gilliss: 15–20 killed at Tunnel 10. Partridge: “a good many were frozen to death.”
- p. 223–224 ¶36: the Canadian Pacific analog: 600 to 3,000 deaths.
- p. 224–225 ¶40–53: a list of reported deaths, 1866–69. Colfax explosion (Apr. 1866); snowslides (Dec. 1866, Mar. 1867, 19+ killed); NY Evening Post, Dec. 1867 (22 killed); Truckee cabin (Jan. 1868, 5); and others.
- **p. 226–227 ¶54 (COMPANY PRIORITIES):** “The almost complete absence of attention to worker fatalities in the correspondence among the CPRR’s top leaders is itself evidence of the low regard.” Clement: “I never counted … never cared about them so long as we got the work done.” **E. B. Crocker to Huntington, Jan. 31, 1867: accidents would come “in spite of all precautions,” but the company must be ready so they “will not stop the tracklaying beyond.”**
- p. 227 ¶55: “the CPRR never issued any public statement acknowledging the death of any railroad worker.”
- **p. 227–228 ¶56–58 (death toll):** possibly 1,200 or more died, based on the June 1870 *Sacramento Reporter*: “accumulated bones of perhaps 1,200 Chinamen … about 20,000 pounds.” The n. concedes a same-day report of about 50 bodies, and that the figure is questioned. **Chang’s own bottom line (p. 230 ¶62): “likely well into the hundreds, if not substantially higher.”** Use that hedged line, not “1,200.”
- p. 229–230 ¶61–62: association records, 1850s–1869: 7.5% died in America. *Railroad Record*: 12%.
- p. 231 ¶65–67: LA massacre, 1871 (18 lynched). Truckee “Trout Creek Outrage” (June 1876, Caucasian League) and the “Truckee method”. Denver, 1880.
- **p. 232 ¶68: ERROR.** Chang: “Congress overrode his veto” (Arthur, 1882). **Wrong.** Arthur vetoed the 20-year bill (Apr. 4, 1882); the override failed; he signed the 10-year Exclusion Act on May 6, 1882. Do not import. Arthur’s veto quote, that Chinese “were largely instrumental in constructing the railways,” is usable once verified.
- p. 232 ¶70: Rock Springs, 1885: 28+ killed, and the victims were **Union Pacific** coal miners. [IVORY: UP/Eastern-owned]
- p. 233 ¶72: about 170 expulsion episodes. The Chinese population fell from 133,000 (1882) to 90,000 (1900).
- p. 233 ¶74–75: Sing Lum oral history: graves around **Delano**, Kern County, on the SP (Delano the town; not a Delano-family crossover, though the town was named for Columbus Delano, Grant’s Interior Secretary [IVORY-adjacent; verify]).
- **p. 234–235 ¶76–77:** Santa Cruz Mountains tunnel explosion (Nov. 18, 1879): 24 to 32 Chinese killed on the line owned by **James G. Fair** (South Pacific Coast RR, San Jose–Santa Cruz). Cardinal: a Peninsula/Stanford-region railroad. Also note Alfred E. Davis (quoted p. 164) was Fair’s partner.

## Conclusion (pp. 237–246): read in full
- p. 237–238 ¶1: at the 1919 50th anniversary, three aged workers were paraded. **Minor error:** Chang puts Susanville “in western Nevada.” It is in Lassen County, California.
- p. 238 ¶2: E. B. Crocker died in 1875, Charles Crocker in 1888, **Stanford in 1893**, Strobridge in 1921.
- p. 238–240 ¶3–7: Hung Wah’s probable end (Placerville county hospital, 1931). His Auburn wash house was dynamited in July 1880 and “public sentiment appears to be not greatly outraged.”
- p. 242–243 ¶13: a descendant is a Stanford undergraduate.
- p. 244 ¶16: descendants are almost all from contractor or headman families.
- p. 244 ¶22: Department of Labor Hall of Honor, 2014; Obama–Xi, 2015.

## Acknowledgments (pp. 247–248): read in full; AUTHOR-CONFLICT disclosure
- **The book rests on “the Chinese Railroad Workers in North America Project at Stanford University, which I have co-directed with Shelley Fisher Fishkin.”** Stanford students did research, and Stanford librarians and Stanford-housed archives helped. **Richard White read drafts** (cross-check: White-*Railroaded* agreement is not fully independent). Julie Cain is thanked (her M.A. thesis is the source for the Stanford-mitigation passages, pp. 61–63). The Huntington Library is thanked.
- Photo credits: Yale Beinecke (Watkins) [IVORY: archive only].

# Cardinal close reading – Denton, The Profiteers

**Citation scheme:** chapter + paragraph (¶) in.

**Book:** Sally Denton, *The Profiteers: Bechtel and the Men Who Built the World* (New York: Simon & Schuster, 2016), ebook ISBN 9781476706481. Cardinal Drive (folder 05).

**Clean extract.** Publisher-made S&S ebook (clean XHTML, no OCR). Working text extracted locally for search (not published). The ebook has no print page-list, so **cite chapter + paragraph number (¶) in our extract**: count body paragraphs from the chapter title, with chapter headings excluded. Endnotes are phrase-keyed, at the back (Notes, by chapter). Quotes are verbatim. The only change: a stray space after opening quotation marks (an ebook link artifact, e.g. “ This”) has been closed up.

---

## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 (night)

### Preface / Prologue (skimmed in full)
- Preface ¶21: Kevin Starr on Bechtel: “an entity so powerful, so international in scope, that its officers . . . could move to the CIA, the Department of Defense, and the Department of State respectively as if they were merely shifting assignments at Bechtel.”
- Preface ¶27: the “Corporate West”: government as primary business partner, “The relationship began with the railroads, especially in California.” Postwar defense construction “would ultimately spin off into the software industry centered in northern California.”
- Prologue: the Pollard frame (Weinberger, Shultz).

### Ch. 1 Go West! (¶1–20)
- ¶1: W. A. Bechtel born September 12, 1872, Freeport IL; to Peabody KS at twelve.
- ¶5–6: Southern Pacific gang foreman, Reno, winter 1902–03; estimator at Wadsworth, $59/month.
- ¶8: 1904 to Oakland; he filled the swamp at the head of Lake Merritt for Lakeshore Park (a land-making contract).
- ¶9: 1906 first own subcontract (Western Pacific, Pleasanton–Sunol); “This independent undertaking marked the birth of the modern Bechtel company.”
- ¶11: Wattis brothers / Utah Construction; Eccles capital; Northwestern Pacific payment “nearly $500,000.”
- ¶14: cites McCartney for the gold mine and toothbrush losses; “The salvation of his fortune and future would lie … with the US government.”
- ¶15: 1919 “first federal highway contract in California” (Klamath River Highway); Sequoia Generals Highway; Yosemite.
- ¶17: 1921 partnership with Henry J. Kaiser; 1929 first PG&E gas line; a fortune of “more than $30 million by the end of the 1920s.”
- ¶19: “When the Herbert Hoover administration announced in 1929 that it would accept bids to dam the Colorado River …” Bids were opened March 4, 1931 (USBR chronology); the 1929 “announcement” is loose. Dad becomes national president of the Associated General Contractors that year.

### Ch. 2 Follow the Water (¶1–12) — HOOVER / STATE POWER
- ¶4: “on a February morning in 1931, a group of twelve West Coast contractors assembled at the Engineers’ Club in San Francisco.”
- ¶6: eight firms; Kaiser named it after Chinatown’s Six Companies; $500,000 each toward the $5 million bond; “The $1.5 million contributed by Bechtel and Kaiser combined gave them a resounding 30 percent equity in the project. Six Companies Inc. was incorporated in Delaware, just two weeks before the bids were to be submitted.” (Bechtel and Kaiser 30%: matches the ledger’s “30 percent, in later standard accounts.”)
- ¶7: “Boulder Dam (renamed Hoover Dam in 1947)”. **Oversimplified:** Wilbur named it Hoover Dam in September 1930; Ickes renamed it Boulder in 1933; the Hoover name was restored in 1947 (Whyte p. 587; ledger 1930-09-17). Denton quotes Nies: the dam was “put in motion by the business-oriented Hoover administration to help the landowners of the Imperial Valley of Southern California” (**land motive**, attributed to Nies).
- ¶8: “On November 24, 1922 … Then–US commerce secretary Herbert Hoover, longtime promoter of public-private partnerships … brokered the contentious gathering.” The Compact was signed that night in Santa Fe. **Agrees with Whyte pp. 270–271** (strengthens CANON-026). Then: “six years later, Congress took control and authorized construction of a dam.”
- ¶10: Crowe, ex-Bureau superintendent (1924), was Six Companies’ “secret weapon”; bid “$48,890,955—coincidentally just $24,000 more than government engineers had calculated”; “on March 4, 1931, the bureau awarded the contract to Six Companies.” **Date conflict:** USBR says bids were opened March 4 and the contract awarded March 11, 1931. Bid figure: McCartney p. 34 gives $48,890,000; USBR gives $48,890,995.50.
- ¶11: “At $165 million, the Boulder Canyon Project Act—signed into law by President Hoover …” **Error:** the Act was signed by Coolidge on December 21, 1928. Hoover took office in March 1929. → canon.

### Ch. 3 Hobo Jungle (¶1–10)
- ¶3: Crowe goes to Las Vegas “A week after Six Companies won the bid.”
- ¶8: Arizona tunnels opened “November 13, 1932”; the river diverted the next morning.
- ¶9: “In June 1933 a giant bucket … dumped the first load” of concrete. **Supports June 1933 against McCartney’s April 10, 1935** (CANON-027; agrees with USBR). Errors in the same paragraph: “60 million tons of concrete” (¶2 itself says a “six-million-ton structure”) and a pour of “nine months” (it ran June 1933 – May 1935).
- ¶10: final diversion gate lowered January 31, 1935; “Completed two and a half years ahead of schedule.” Roger Morris quote: “joining public purpose and private enrichment in a marriage the West . . . took for granted.”

### Ch. 4 That Hellhole (¶1–17)
- ¶2: Six Companies executive committee headed by Bechtel; Steve “vice president of Six Companies and was in charge of purchasing.” Contract paid $8 per cubic yard against a $5.50 cost; $850 per Boulder City house against a $145 build cost; surety bond recovered by early 1932.
- ¶4: Six Companies “deliberately misdiagnosed” carbon-monoxide deaths as pneumonia. ¶6: at least fifty CO cases settled privately.
- ¶7: August 1931 strike; “the Hoover administration was obsequious toward the contractors”; Asians and African Americans barred.
- ¶8: Boulder City voted 78% for FDR in 1932 (quoting Stevens).
- ¶9: Ickes fines $350,000, reduced to $100,000.
- ¶10: Six Companies profit “more than $10 million” (Fortune, ch. 2 ¶11, estimated $7 million).
- **¶14: Dad died “on the night of August 28, 1933” at the National Hotel, Moscow; insulin overdose; “fifteen days shy of his sixty-first birthday.”** A second source for CANON-028.
- ¶16: Steve becomes president “after a brief power struggle.”

### Ch. 5 Wartime Socialists (¶1–17)
- ¶2: sons given 5% each “upon incorporation in 1925 of W. A. Bechtel Co.” **Internal conflict:** ch. 1 ¶9 says incorporation came “another sixteen years” after 1906, i.e. 1922. Unsettled.
- ¶3–5: Steve born September 24, 1900; Berkeley from 1918; on November 8, 1919 his car killed a mother and daughter (the Chappels); charged with manslaughter, never prosecuted (quoting McCartney).
- ¶6: married Laura Peart in 1923; lived in an Art Deco building near Lake Merritt that Dad’s partners had built.
- ¶9: McCone born January 4, 1902, a year behind Steve at Berkeley; at Consolidated Steel 1931; “Consolidated had supplied Six Companies with fifty-five million tons of steel.” **Repeats McCartney’s implausible figure (CANON-029).** Derivative, not independent.

The Hoover Presidential Library adds that the bill “was largely written by Hoover and Secretary of the Interior Hubert Work.” Effective June 25, 1929. → Denton ch. 2 ¶11 is wrong on the signer, but Hoover’s drafting role is real.
- **SRI origin:** SRI’s own corporate history (archived 2017): in **1925** “Dr. Robert E. Swain … championed the idea of an interdisciplinary research institute … Early supporters included Stanford alumnus and trustee, Herbert Hoover.” In 1927 Wilbur recommended a plan; it was tabled in 1930; in **1939** “Stanford’s faculty committee discussed the institute idea while meeting at the Bohemian Grove”; Atholl McBean was acknowledged as founder “along with the Stanford University Board of Trustees”; articles were filed **November 6, 1946**; “Stanford University trustees elected 11 SRI directors.” SRI’s 2022 heritage chapter says the charter let the trustees select SRI’s directors, and the initial directors were “32 of the most prestigious western executives.” SRI’s 75th-anniversary story says Swain pitched Hoover (“then Secretary of Commerce”) in the late 1920s, and “Hoover was enthusiastic.” → Denton’s “Initially conceived by President Hoover” overstates it: the idea was Swain’s, and Hoover was an early backer as trustee and Commerce Secretary, not President. Bechtel as a founding director rests on Gibson p. 156 (via Denton). Not yet independently seen.
- **Hoover Institution and Bechtel money (modern, verified):** Stephen D. Bechtel Jr. made “a five-year $5 million pledge for a new building at Hoover” (*Inside Philanthropy*, April 21, 2015). He was a named donor to the Traitel Building (hoover.org, March 13 and July 6, 2017). The **S. D. Bechtel, Jr. Foundation** helped fund the **George P. Shultz Building** (hoover.org, March 1, 2024). Denton’s *1970s* claim (ch. 20 ¶10) remains unsourced.

## Cross-book synthesis (Denton vs Whyte, McCartney, canon)
1. **Denton depends heavily on McCartney** for 1898–1987 (dozens of notes cite *Friends in High Places* by page). Where they agree, Denton is not independent corroboration unless her note cites something else. Independent Denton sources: declassified Kissinger/Ford telcons (1976), State Department cables (Mindanao workers), Gibson’s SRI history, IPS/*WaPo* Aqaba documents, Bechtel’s website.
2. **SRI–Hoover–Bechtel:** the strongest Stanford “intent” material in Denton is ch. 10 ¶4–5 plus ch. 12 ¶1–2, 10. SRI is “Bechtel-dominated,” with Steve Sr. pushing international work “doubled and doubled,” Ex-Im projects “researched and selected by SRI,” and the Nixon Pacific Rim strategy “spawned at” SRI. This is a pattern of use, not a document showing Stanford decided anything for Bechtel’s benefit. It is not a smoking gun.
3. **Errors in Denton** (dates and officeholders): Boulder Act signer; March 4 vs 11, 1931; 60M tons and nine months (ch. 3); Forrestal–McCone 1950; McCone AEC 1957 and DCI “after 1962”; Shultz “colonel”; Davis “head of the AEC”; Iraq terror-list date (1982 vs November 1983); 430 vs 440 layoffs; FUSRAP origin; Shultz board list (World Bank/IMF). Cite Denton for characterization and for her unique documents, not for dates.
4. **Whyte agreement:** Denton’s November 24, 1922 Colorado River Compact brokered by Hoover agrees with Whyte.
5. **Hoover and the Grove (settled against Whyte p. 337):** Whyte quotes Hoover’s 1925 letter to Mark Sullivan: the encampment “has now become the greatest men’s party in the world.” So Denton’s ch. 10 ¶14 attribution is substantially right, though Denton has “on earth” and Whyte’s primary-letter wording is “in the world.” Whyte also shows Hoover *at the Grove* in August 1927 when the wire report of Coolidge’s “I do not choose” statement reached him. Afterwards he “remained at his cabinet post, refusing to declare a candidacy.” So Denton’s “It was at the Grove that Herbert Hoover had announced his presidential candidacy” (ch. 10 ¶17) is **wrong as stated**. The defensible version: the Grove was where Hoover and his intimates learned of Coolidge’s withdrawal and began “to spin out theories” (Whyte’s phrase is “Like so many weaving spiders,” and Denton’s ch. 10 title borrows the Grove motto).

# Cardinal close reading – McCartney, Friends in High Places

**Book:** Laton McCartney, *Friends in High Places: The Bechtel Story: The Most Secret Corporation and How It Engineered the World* (New York: Simon and Schuster, 1988). ISBN 0-671-47415-4; LCCN 87-34562. Cardinal Drive (folder 05).

**Copy check (21 Nov 2026, 7:50 PM PT):** Drive search for the title returns only this EPUB (5,933,837 bytes, same size and bytes as the local copy) and the older notes Doc. No newer or cleaner copy exists in Drive.

**Clean extract.** The EPUB is a 2011 pdftohtml conversion of a scan of the 1988 S&S first edition. Its ~1,890 PNGs are blank scanner-noise tiles, not page images, so OCR of page images is impossible. The OCR text layer is in reading order for body paragraphs; only chapter-opening paragraphs (drop-cap blocks) are scrambled, and footnotes are interleaved where the page broke. Working text extracted locally (not published), with `[[p. N]]` print-page markers recovered from the printed folios. Normalizations only: whitespace; split-letter OCR joins (“W ith” → “With”) where the joined word occurs elsewhere in the book; endnote numbers shown as `[nN]`; running heads removed. **Quotes below are verbatim from that OCR layer except those normalizations.** OCR quirks kept as-is: em dashes appear as hyphens (“secrecy-in the early 1970s”), “BechtelMcCone” for Bechtel-McCone, “W A. Bechtel” for W. A. Bechtel. Opening paragraphs of each chapter are not quoted unless reconstructed.

**Missing pages in this copy (scan gaps, confirmed by text discontinuity + running heads):** pp. 32–33, 64–65, 96–97, 116–117, 130, 132–133, 164–165, 180–181 (15 pp.). p. 32–33 is the Six Companies formation; p. 165 is the opening of ch. 15 “Secretary Shultz.” Anything on those pages is **not read** and must not be cited to this copy.

**Citation scheme:** print page of the 1988 Simon & Schuster first edition (folios printed in the scan), plus chapter. Endnote numbers are McCartney's per-chapter notes (Notes, pp. 240–257).
