## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 (evening) — Chapters 1–6 (pp. 11–80)

### Ch. 1 The Grove (pp. 11–17)
- 1982 frame: Stephen D. Bechtel Jr. driven to the Bohemian Grove the last weekend of July 1982. p. 13: “a secluded, 2, 700-acre stand of redwoods 75 miles east of San Francisco. It was named the Bohemian Grove.” **Geography error in McCartney:** the Grove (Monte Rio) is north of San Francisco, not east. Quote the acreage, not the bearing.
- p. 12: Bechtel Group “the largest engineering and construction company in the world”; footnote: renamed Bechtel Group in 1979.
- p. 12: Bechtel “had been influencing presidents since Herbert Hoover.”
- p. 13 footnote (interleaved): Shultz opened the company to press; Bechtel “now publishes its yearly revenues.”
- p. 14: Ehrlichman: “Once you’ve spent three days with someone in an informal situation … you have a relationship-a relationship that opens doors and makes it easier to pick up the phone.”[n3]
- p. 14: Grove friends “had provided the contacts and the contracts … and on occasion, skirted the law.” Footnote p. 14: family sources estimate 1982 fortunes: Sr. $1 billion; Jr. $600–700 million.
- pp. 14–15: Mandalay camp roster includes Shultz, Kissinger, McCone, Wm. French Smith, Edgar Kaiser Jr., Flanigan, Halaby, Cooley (Wells Fargo), Nicholas Brady, Gerald Ford. Other 1982 Grove guests: **David Packard** (“computer magnate (and former deputy Defense secretary)”), Volcker, Webster, Haig, Hearst Jr., SP president Alan Furth.
- p. 15: Dillon, Read — “the Wall Street brokerage house in which Bechtel had a controlling interest.” Southern Pacific “had given Bechtel some of its earliest business.”
- p. 16: Ford, Nixon, Reagan each tried “to give Bechtel commercial access to the nation’s most secret nuclear technology”; Bechtel “providing ‘cover’ and intelligence for the CIA.”
- p. 17: Weinberger (general counsel) to Defense; Shultz named Secretary of State three weeks before the 1982 Grove.

### Ch. 2 Dad (pp. 18–28)
- p. 18: Warren A. Bechtel born September 12, 1872, Freeport, Illinois; family to Peabody, Kansas, 1884.
- pp. 19–20: bankrupt on cattle feeding; grades track for the Rock Island in Indian Territory at $2.75/day. Stephen Davison Bechtel born September 14, 1900 (Indiana).
- p. 20: winter 1902–03, Reno: “I landed in Reno with a wife, two babies, a slide trombone and a ten-dollar bill”[n1]; hired by Southern Pacific (A. J. Barkley) at $55 a month.
- p. 21: c. 1903–04 to Oakland for E. B. & A. L. Stone (Richmond Belt Railroad; Santa Fe into Oakland).
- p. 22: after the 1906 earthquake buys a Marion Model 20 steam shovel, paints “W A. BECHTEL Co.”; age 34.
- p. 23: Wattis brothers (Utah Construction), Mormons who “many believed, the State of Utah as well.”
- p. 24: 1914 last 106 miles of the Northwestern Pacific; final check “nearly $500,000.”
- p. 25: investments: Arizona copper mine; Industrial Indemnity (cofounded 1920, SF); “several large tracts of real estate he purchased in downtown Oakland and San Francisco.” Port Orford, Oregon placer mine enjoined after dairy farmers sued over silt in the Sixes River — “the first of many clashes the Bechtels would have with environmentalists.”
- p. 26: 1919 “the first federal public-road contract let in California: the building of the Klamath River Highway.”
- pp. 26–27: Henry J. Kaiser partnership, summer 1921; 50/50, handshake (Kaiser quote p. 27 [n10]).
- p. 28: pipelines for Standard Oil, then Continental Gas; by end of 1920s “a fortune approaching $30 million.” Lake Merritt high-rise.

### Ch. 3 Boulder (pp. 29–42) — HIGH PRIORITY (pp. 32–33 missing)
- p. 29: Kaiser’s 1928 $20 million Cuba road contract; dreams of the Colorado dam.
- pp. 29–30 (footnote running into body): “Nothing, that is, until 1930, when a former engineer from California named Herbert Hoover decided, as president, that it was worth a go. Under his aegis, funds for the project had been allocated, and the U.S. Department of Reclamation had announced that it would soon be accepting construction bids.” **Conflict with Whyte pp. 270–271:** Hoover’s Boulder role starts in 1922 as Commerce Secretary chairing the Colorado River Compact talks around a Bureau of Reclamation Boulder Canyon report. McCartney compresses this into “1930 … as president” and misnames the Bureau. See CANON-026.
- p. 30: Bowman Dam (W. A. Bechtel Co., managed by Warren Jr.) “the second-largest rock-fill dam in the world.”
- p. 31: **Leland Cutler**, “a prominent San Francisco banker and an old friend and schoolmate of Herbert Hoover’s,” told Morrison the winner must post “a $5 million surety bond” and suggested partners (Felix Kahn). Cardinal link: a Hoover/Stanford-circle banker is the matchmaker for Six Companies. (Cutler’s Stanford class is not given here — needs second source.)
- p. 31: Crowe “had drawn up the original estimates for Boulder” twenty years before.
- p. 34: officers: [W. H. Wattis president], E. O. Wattis second VP; Shea field construction; Kahn finance; Crowe superintendent. Bid set at Wattis’s hospital bedside: Crowe’s figures “then added 25 percent. If all went well, this would be their profit.”
- p. 34: bid filed in Denver March 4 [1931]: “It totaled $48,890,000-$5 million below the nextlowest bid, $10 million below the highest and only $24,000 above the government’s own estimates.”
- p. 34 footnote: Marriner Eccles (Utah Construction part-owner, Ogden banker’s son; Fed chairman 1936–48) had “a close personal and professional relationship with the Bechtel family.”
- p. 36: Bechtel elected Six Companies president “after W H. Wattis succumbed to cancer in September 1931”; contract had “performance incentives.”
- pp. 36–37: materials, high-scalers, diversion tunnels.
- p. 38: executive committee Bechtel/Kaiser/Shea/Kahn; Kaiser “chief lobbyist … dispatched to Washington.” Strike: workers charged half their $4/day for board and tent; 13 dead of heat prostration.
- pp. 38–39: Crowe: “We are six months ahead of schedule’ … and we can afford to refuse concessions which would cost us $2,000 daily or $3 million in the seven years we are allowed to finish the work.”[n8] Aug 10 [1931] all strikers fired; troops from Fort Douglas.
- p. 39: “The Hoover administration, which tended to view any labor disturbance as ‘Red-inspired,’ was unsympathetic.”
- pp. 39–40: by early 1932 the $5 million surety recouped plus $1 million incentives; contract paid “an $8 charge for every cubic yard of earth excavated, when … it was costing Six Companies a third less.”
- p. 40: April [1932] Hoover “failed to ask Congress for sufficient funds”; Kaiser lobbies a deficit appropriation.
- p. 40: Sen. Oddie: scrip pay and “two sets of books.” McCartney: “What stung more, they were true.”
- pp. 40–41: Ickes: 70,000 violations, fine $350,000, cut to $100,000 after Kaiser’s PR blitz.
- **Internal date error:** p. 40 has concrete pouring ready “by the spring of 1935” and p. 41 “On April 10, 1935, the final phase … the pouring of the. first concrete,” yet p. 42 says all 3.25 million yards were poured “by the summer of 1935” and quotes “Twelve hundred men … had in 21 months built a structure.” Standard accounts (Stevens 1988) date first concrete June 6, 1933. Treat McCartney’s 1935 first-pour date as an error. CANON-027.
- p. 41: Black workers barred until 1933; refused Boulder City housing.
- p. 42: Sept 30, 1935 FDR dedication.

### Ch. 4 Steve (pp. 43–55)
- p. 43: partners’ profits “between $1 million and $2 million” each after Crowe’s $300,000 bonus.
- p. 44: Bay Bridge “$11. 5 million and more than 50 lives” [OCR; figure as printed]. Bridge Builders, Inc. (Kaisers + Bechtels) vs. Transbay Construction.
- p. 45: Warren A. Bechtel dies in Moscow, National Hotel, **August 28, 1933**, insulin overdose, en route to inspect the Dnieper dam. (Ledger has 1933-01-01 placeholder → fix to 1933-08-28. CANON-028.)
- p. 46: company incorporated 1925; Dad gave each son 5 percent; stock fight with Steve and Ken before his death.
- p. 46 footnote: Robert L. Bridges (Thelen, Marrin) advised Steve against Dad, later Bechtel chief counsel.
- p. 47: Steve, after Oakland Technical High and the 20th Engineers in France, “enrolled at the University of California at Berkeley in 1918.”
- pp. 47–48: Nov 1919 car crash at Moss and Broadway killed Mrs. Jessie Chappel and Elizabeth Chappel; manslaughter charge stricken (quotes Oakland Tribune, Nov 17, 1919). Footnote: company literature hid that he attended UC and did not graduate.
- p. 48: married Laura Adaline Peart, September 1923; Stephen D. Jr. born May 10, 1925.
- p. 49: Steve “chief of administration” at Boulder (purchasing); Crowe called him “terribly ambitious.”
- p. 50: 1936 S. D. Bechtel Company (Steve + Ken). Broadway Tunnel $3.9 million contract — “too damn low … half of what it should have been.” (McCartney says the “Department of Reclamation” let it; doubtful. Flag, low priority.)
- p. 51: Steve: “competitive work for the government was unpredictable … many contractors went broke pursuing it.”[n11]
- p. 52: McCone (Berkeley engineering, 10th in class) a year behind Steve.
- pp. 52–53: McCone, sales manager at Consolidated Steel (1931), sells Boulder steel through old friend Steve, who ran purchasing: “Consolidated eventually supplied Boulder with a total of 55 million tons of steel.” **Implausible figure** (p. 36 gives 45 million *pounds* of reinforcing steel for the whole dam). Do not use “55 million tons.” CANON-029.
- p. 53: Bechtel-McCone Corporation, Los Angeles, **May 1937** — McCone president, Bechtel chairman with control. Supports ledger 1937-05-01.
- pp. 54–55: Socal Richmond refinery; Parsons (BMP 1938, out 1944); by 1939 >10,000 employees.

### Ch. 5 The War Years (pp. 56–70) (pp. 64–65 missing)
- pp. 56–57: summer 1940 lunch; Adm. Howard L. Vickery (Maritime Commission) needs 60 tankers for the British; Roach steers him to Bechtel and McCone.
- p. 58: Richmond and Marinship (Sausalito); Calship (Terminal Island) first contract January 11, 1942.
- p. 59: Calship 42,000 workers. George S. Cooley Jr., in Manila spring 1941 for naval base and airfield work; captured in Borneo (Philippines link for Kyle’s Philippine-war thread).
- p. 61: Calship 20 ships in October 1944 — “the most productive single shipyard in the world.”
- pp. 61–63: Canol pipeline: Somervell; 10 percent guaranteed profit; Stimson: “This is what your country has decided you are going to do during the war.”[n8] $25 million hidden “in a massive war appropriations bill” to keep it from Ickes.
- p. 66: Canol finished May 1945; oil at $150/barrel; cost “more than $134 million.”
- pp. 66–69: “Willow Run” aircraft modification plant near Birmingham, Alabama: cost plus 5 percent on BechtelMcCone’s own six-month estimates; qui tam suit by George P. Alexander, July 31, 1943; dismissed when the contract produced in court read “fixed fee.” McCone to Fortune (May 17, 1943, unpublished): “a fee of five percent of the estimated amount of work regardless … of how much work we actually do turn out.”[n21] McCartney: “If McCone’s memory was, in fact, accurate, the contract wording, it seemed, had been changed.” Profit $3,375,000. (Name check: the Birmingham Aircraft Modification Center is usually not called “Willow Run,” which was Ford’s Michigan plant. Flag as possible McCartney naming error; unverified.)
- p. 70: GAO: Calship revenues $44,423,014; Marinship $11.8 million; $23.55 million from equity in Kaiser shipbuilding; gross “well over $100 million. Their net investment: considerably less than $400,000.”
- p. 70 footnote: Cooley killed in Baghdad, 1958 revolution.

### Ch. 6 In His Own Image (pp. 71–80) — HIGH PRIORITY (Simpson/Hoover; SRI)
- p. 71: Steve’s fortune “in the same league as the Huntingtons, Crockers and Stanfords”; by 1946 a leading member of the Pacific Union and Bohemian clubs, which had excluded Dad.
- p. 72 footnote: Steve bought large blocks of client stock (Socal); portfolio “worth hundreds of millions.”
- p. 73: Bechtel men “Virtually all had been born in California and educated at Berkeley, Stanford or USC.”
- pp. 73–74: **John L. Simpson** (Laura’s uncle): after Berkeley worked for the Commission for Relief in Belgium; five years in Europe; “developing a close friendship with CRB’s head and his fellow San Franciscan, Herbert Hoover.” Then J. Henry Schroder Banking Corp.; with the Dulles brothers via Sullivan & Cromwell (p. 74). Hoover–CRB–Schroder–Dulles–Bechtel chain. Compare Whyte on CRB (CANON-019).
- p. 74 footnote: Schroder family; Baron Bruno von Schröder’s 1932 Hitler–von Papen meeting [as McCartney tells it]; bank also gave OSS cover.
- p. 75: Simpson’s private intelligence to Acheson and Donovan; in 1943–44 “in effect controlled” Italy’s treasury for the Army.
- p. 76: 1946 Simpson becomes Bechtel CFO and “eminence grise”; HQ 153 Sansome.
- p. 76: Steve: “We’d rather be known to a hundred key people than to a hundred million.”[n8] → “the sweetheart clients.”
- pp. 76–77: PG&E’s James B. Black got Steve onto the J. P. Morgan board and into the Business Council.
- **p. 78 — SRI as a sales tool (closest thing to a smoking gun in Run 1):** for the Trans Mountain pipeline pitch, “Bechtel commissioned a study of the potential for oil usage in the Pacific Northwest from the Stanford Research Institute of Palo Alto. That the study would produce a favorable conclusion Bechtel was more than reasonably certain: he had been one of SRI’s principal founders and had bankrolled its operations heavily. Sure enough, SRI turned in a study fairly glowing with […]”
- **p. 78 footnote:** “Founded in 1946 by a group of West Coast businessmen, including Steve Bechtel and Henry J. Kaiser, and originally affiliated with Stanford University, the Stanford Research Institute eventually grew to become the second-largest corporate-government ‘think tank’ in the country.” Work on strategic forces, ballistic missile defense, Sputnik response; Vietnam-era defense work “provoked violent student demonstrations on the Stanford University campus, and led the university to sever its connections with the institute in 1969.” “SRI has conducted numerous studies for the company, including evaluating the development potential of Jubail, Saudi Arabia, and drawing up a blueprint for Bechtel’s industrialization of Indonesia during the Sukarno regime. Over the years, the Bechtel family has donated millions to SRI and was principally responsible for the funds used to build SRI’s 4 2, 000-square-foot headquarters which opened in […]” Six Bechtel entities among 68 SRI “associate members”; “No other company or family matches this total.” Source per Notes ch. 6: “SRI papers and annual reports.” CANON-030.
- p. 79: Trans Mountain Pipeline Company of Canada; 718 miles; finished 1954; $93 million; Bechtel $200 million revenue in the first year.
- p. 79: BP Haifa refinery cancelled in 1948; executives say the loss fed “the company’s growing anti-Semitism.”
- p. 80: Steve: “we are not in the construction and engineering business. We are in the business of making money.”

## Run 2 — 2026-11-21 (night) — Chapters 7–21 + Notes skim (pp. 81–257)

### Ch. 7 Saudi Arabia (pp. 81–93)
- Socal concession July 1933 via Philby. McCartney geography slips (Bahrain placed "in the Red Sea"; Jeddah treated as the capital). Don't take geography from this chapter.
- p. 85: after Bechtel "pledged not to hire “Jewish elements”[n3] and to switch the pipeline’s terminus from Egypt to Lebanon," ibn Saud "readily gave the project his assent." (n3 = Childs dispatch 12/3/47, State Dept files.)
- pp. 87–88 footnote: "Cooley’s duties included screening prospective employees to ensure that none were Jewish. The exclusion of Jews from Bechtel projects was quietly sanctioned by the State Deparbnent [sic OCR], which at the time did not employ Jews in Saudi Arabia either."
- p. 89: May 1948 visit "by Steve Bechtel and his son, Steve junior, then just 23 and fresh out of the Marine Corps and Purdue." **Conflicts with p. 131** ("following graduation from Stanford in 194 7"). Settled → CANON-032.
- pp. 92–93: Bechtel lobbyist A. J. Shaw also representing the Saudi government in Washington (Hart dispatch 4/13/49). Source base for the chapter: "State Department files in the National Archives" (Notes, ch. 7).

### Ch. 8 Lucky Man (pp. 94–100; pp. 96–97 missing)
- 1950 revenues ~$200M/yr; Orinoco iron ore; McCone on the Air Policy Commission; 1948 Dulles dinner via Simpson; McCone in Paris helps Eisenhower declare a Republican (Jan 1951).
- **Index lists SRI at p. 97 — a missing page.** The ledger’s "McCartney also records him [McCone] as a director of the Stanford Research Institute" is **not found in any readable page** of this copy; it may sit on p. 97. Unverified here → CANON-031.

### Ch. 9 Atoms for Peace (pp. 101–112)
- p. 103: Lawrence’s MTA at Livermore subcontracted to Bechtel via Socal’s California Research. EBR-1 (Dec 1949).
- p. 104: AEC officials (Davis, Brown, White, O’Donnell) "would leave the agency and ultimately work for Bechtel," prompting Ribicoff: an industry "so incestuous, it is impossible to tell where the public sector begins and the private one leaves off."
- McCone at the AEC from 1958; Caltech trustee; uranium bought from US firms only; Savannah River; McCone’s wish for atomic explosives for Bechtel work refused.
- p. 112: Eisenhower to Bechtel after 1956: "I know you did a lot of work in the recently concluded political campaign and that, in addition, you helped materially on the financial end."[n20]

### Ch. 10 The Company and The Company (pp. 113–125; pp. 116–117 missing) — STATE POWER
- 1947 Navy intelligence at Ras Tanura; 1948 refinery-demolition plan; 1949 Syrian coup (Childs: "multinational corporation" likely International Bechtel).
- p. 118: Simpson to Allen Dulles: "Occasionally a private concern can perform a function or develop certain aspects of a problem with greater facility than a government agency." Mulligan (1987 interview): operations "loaded with CIA …. Bechtel was delighted to take them on." Libya cover employment 1963–70; Jan 1962 Dulles→Simpson letter on cover for Jens Jebsen (Princeton, Dulles papers).
- pp. 118–119: "In March 1951 … Bechtel became a charter member of the National Committee for a Free Asia … The brainchild of Allen Dulles, NCFA, which later changed its name to the Asia Foundation." (CIA front disclosed 1967.) Bechtel as CIA liaison to the Business Council; McCone Indonesia briefings 1964–65.

### Ch. 11 The Succession (pp. 126–134; pp. 130, 132–133 missing) — STANFORD
- 1958 Fortune net worth $250M.
- **p. 128 footnote:** "The Bechtel family’s numerous and generous charitable contributions are with few exceptions tied in one way or another to business. Among the recipients … the University of California at Berkeley (where Steve senior, who failed to graduate, contributed most of the money that built the Stephen D. Bechtel School of Engineering); Stanford University’s International Student Center, The Ford Foundation and […]" Ties to ledger 1963 Bechtel International Center row (characterization, not date).
- **p. 131:** "They also approved of Steve junior’s enrollment in the MBA program at Stanford, where he came under the tutelage of Paul Holden … following graduation from Stanford in 194 7, Steve announced he was going into business for himself, building houses on the Menlo Park peninsula." Year wrong (MBA 1948) → CANON-032. Menlo Park housing plan is a usable land detail (attributed).

### Ch. 12 Taking Command (pp. 135–142) — SRI #2
- **pp. 136–137:** India fertilizer, 1964: the Indians wanted a feasibility study. "Fine, replied Steve; he’d have the Stanford Research Institute produce one. The $400,000 study (paid for by the Indians) came back confirming Bechtel’s opinions, and then some: not only would one fertilizer plant be good for India, it said, but five-all to be built by Bechtel-would be even better." ### Ch. 13 Libya (pp. 143–151)

### Ch. 14 A Friend in the White House (pp. 152–164; p. 164 missing) — HOOVER + SRI #3
- Revenues $750M (1968) → ~$2B (1974). Alaska pipeline management contract Feb 1974, fired May 1975.
- **p. 156:** Kearns (Eximbank) and Bechtel "had met in 1955, when Kearns was serving on the Hoover Commission on Intelligence." Steve Sr. on the bank’s advisory committee from May 1969.

# Miller, *Why Fish Don't Exist* (Simon & Schuster, 2020): Cardinal reading notes

**Book:** Miller, *Why Fish Don't Exist* (Simon & Schuster, 2020)

**Citation scheme:** print page from S&S 2020 ebook page_N anchors [[p. N]] + ¶ within section; endnotes in extract.

- **Copy:** publisher epub from Kyle's Cardinal Drive folder (ISBN 9781501160370). Working text extracted locally (not published), with print-page markers and endnotes keyed to the text.
- **Method (lean mode, Nov 21, 2026):**
  - Close-read the Stanford, Jordan, university and eugenics material: ch. 4 pp. 49–59; ch. 5 pp. 68–71; ch. 6 pp. 73–79; ch. 9 pp. 107–123; ch. 10 pp. 125–141; and the endnotes for those pages.
  - Skimmed the memoir chapters (Miller's own life, chs. 1–3, 7–8, 11–13, epilogue). They have no Stanford content.
- **What the book is:** part memoir, part biography of David Starr Jordan. It draws heavily on Cutler, *The Mysterious Death of Jane Stanford* (2003), Carnochan (American Scholar, 2003), Spoehr (dissertation, 1975), Lombardo and Jordan's own *Days of a Man* (1922). Treat it as a secondary synthesis. The archival citations come mostly secondhand.


## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 — Lean mode: close-read ch 4 pp. 49–59, ch 5 pp. 68–71, ch 6 pp. 73–79, ch 9 pp. 107–123, ch 10 pp. 125–141 + their endnotes; memoir chapters skimmed…

## Top findings for Cardinal
1. **The Bloomington visit was March 21–22, 1891, not 1890** (CANON-108).
   - Miller (pp. 53–54) says "one day in 1890," and our ledger, timeline and ep4-02 copied that.
   - McMains (*Indiana Magazine of History* 115, Sept. 2019) and Stanford Magazine date it: the Stanfords arrived Saturday, March 21, 1891, and Jordan accepted Sunday, March 22. Jordan was IU's president, and 40.
   - Fixed in the drafts and the ledger.
2. **Jane Stanford vs. Jordan, 1904: the Goebel letters** (CANON-109).
   - Jane used German professor Julius Goebel as an informant.
   - On June 6, 1904, Goebel wrote to her accusing Jordan of "whitewashing" Charles Gilbert's affair and of running the university like a "gang" (Horace Davis Papers SC0028, via Carnochan).
   - Jane wrote to the senior trustee that Jordan's moral failings had "been painfully evident to me for a long time."
   - Spoehr: by the end of 1904 "rumors abounded that Mrs. Stanford planned to replace Jordan" (pp. 69–71).
3. **Jordan in Honolulu, March 1905** (CANON-110).
   - He told the NYT (Mar. 11, 1905) the trip had "nothing whatever to do with the investigation."
   - He paid Dr. Ernest Waterhouse $350. Waterhouse never examined the body, but his memo for Jordan said he was "decidedly not" convinced of poisoning.
   - Jordan's statement offered gingerbread, exertion and angina, then "hysteria."
   - The Honolulu doctors answered: "It is imbecile to think…" Jordan attacked Dr. Humphris as "a man without professional or personal standing" and called the doctors' diagnosis a money-making conspiracy.
   - To Carl S. Smith (Mar. 24, 1905): "morally certain" (pp. 112–117).
4. **The jury's words:** strychnine "introduced into a bottle of bicarbonate of soda with felonious intent by some person or persons to this jury unknown" (p. 112, via Cutler 45). The SF *Evening Bulletin* headline of March 1, 1905, MRS. STANFORD DIES, POISONED, printed the finding ahead of the jury.
5. **Aftermath** (CANON-111):
   - After Jordan fired Goebel, the trustees stripped his power to dismiss faculty (Spoehr).
   - In 1913 he was moved to chancellor. This matches Whyte p. 124, where Hoover engineered it; Miller doesn't mention Hoover.
6. **Eugenics as Jordan's program** (CANON-112):
   - In the 1880s at Indiana he taught that "pauperism" could be "exterminated just as swamps are drained."
   - He published on eugenics from 1898: *Blood of the Nation*, *Human Harvest*, *Your Family Tree*.
   - Indiana passed its 1907 law (his "friends from Bloomington"). Miller says he "helped get" California's 1909 law passed.
   - He chaired the American Breeders Association's Eugenics Committee.
   - Miller says he persuaded **Mary Harriman** to give more than $500,000 for the Eugenics Record Office. Standard accounts credit Davenport; Jordan's memoir (vol. 2, pp. 297–98) is the basis for his role, so hedge it.
7. **Strychnine in Jordan's *Guide to the Study of Fishes* (1905), p. 430**, under "How to Secure Fishes" (CANON-113). Suggestive only; Miller presents it as a discovery, not proof.
8. **Scholarly range on the death** (useful for the Disputes tab):
   - Cutler: poisoned; Jordan covered it up.
   - Carnochan: Jordan "had the motive."
   - White: suspects Bertha Berner (for the will money); Jordan covered up; the death was "lucky" for him.
   - Spoehr: poisoned, but Jordan ordering it is "fantasy."
   - A retired Stanford archivist: Cutler is "speculation."

## Conflicts with the Cardinal drafts (and what was done)
- Ledger 1890-01-01, timeline l.47, ep4-02 l.67 and moments.md l.46 had 1890. **Fixed** to Mar 21–22, 1891 and rekeyed the ledger/art to 1891-03-22.
- ep4-02 l.69 had "Jordan was thirty-nine." **Fixed** to forty.
- ep5-03 l.33 cited "(Miller 2018)." **Fixed** to Miller 2020, ch. 9, pp. 112–117.
- Timeline l.63 (Jordan sails, backs "natural causes," cites Miller ch. 9): consistent.
- Ledger 1905 row (Waterhouse, contested): consistent. Miller adds the $350 fee and the "morally certain" letter; optional.
- ch/3-03 (ABA eugenics committee chair; 1909 law): consistent. If the Harriman/ERO gift is added, hedge it.

## Do not import from Miller
- "One day in 1890" (it was March 1891).
- "Just a year into David's presidency, Leland Stanford had died." Leland died June 21, 1893, about two years in (CANON-115).
- Jordan "persuaded" Mary Harriman, as a flat fact. Attribute it: "by his own account."
- Any suggestion that Jordan caused the death. Miller herself doesn't claim it.

## Ivory crossovers
- **Mary W. Harriman** (E. H. Harriman's widow; mother of Averell and Roland Harriman, both Yale/Skull and Bones) funded the ERO in 1910, which Jordan says he urged. A Stanford-to-Harriman link in eugenics.
- **Andrew D. White** (Cornell; Yale 1853, Skull and Bones) steered the Stanfords to Jordan (from the McMains / Stanford Magazine check, not Miller).
- Agassiz / Harvard (Penikese) as Jordan's model; Yale is not directly involved.

## Leads for other books
- **White, *Who Killed Jane Stanford?*:** Goebel letters, Waterhouse $350, NYT Mar. 11, the Humphris attack, Berner. Cross-check every Miller detail and confirm the inquest date.
- **Harris:** Jordan's eugenics and Terman. Check Harris for the 1909 law's sponsors.
- **Baker:** echoes of the Jordan Hall renaming (2020).

# Cardinal close reading – White, Railroaded

**Citation scheme:** chapter/section + paragraph (¶) in.

**Book:** Richard White, *Railroaded: The Transcontinentals and the Making of Modern America* (New York: W. W. Norton, 2011), ebook ISBN 9780393082609. Cardinal Drive (folder 01).

**Clean extract.** Publisher Norton ebook (clean HTML, no OCR). Working text extracted locally for search (not published). The ebook has no print page-list, so **cite chapter (or Intro / interlude “dmNN” / Epilogue / Conclusion) + ¶** in our extract. Endnote markers appear as [nN] and are keyed to the Notes section (NOT01/NOT01A/NOT01B). Quotes are verbatim. Drop caps in the ebook split a word’s first letter (“F ittingly”); that space is closed up when quoting.

**Method.** Every chapter and interlude was read paragraph by paragraph. The interludes (dm01–dm11) are White’s short biographical vignettes (“A Railroad Life” etc.) and were read too.

---


## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 — All: Introduction; chs 1-11 and dm01-dm11 paragraph by paragraph; Epilogue; Conclusion; Appendix/abbreviations; endnotes checked for every cited…

## Front matter
- Illustrations list (fm03 ¶4, 6, 9, 10, 15–17): many plates come from Stanford University Libraries, Special Collections. ¶10: *The Wasp*, February 19, 1881, “In the Hollow of His Hand”: “Carried by the railroads, Charles Crocker and Collis Huntington support Leland Stanford, who, in turn, holds the Railroad Commission … in the hollow of his hand.”
- Acknowledgments ¶2, ¶5: White researched in Stanford’s Green Library (Margaret Kimball, Jim Kent). Mellon funded the **Spatial History Project at Stanford**, which made many of the book’s maps. White was a Stanford professor, so the book’s interest is disclosed.

## Introduction (¶1–40) — CORE THESIS; STANFORD
- ¶6: “The transcontinentals, more obviously than other railroads, were entwined with the state. Governments subsidized them, secured their rights of way, regulated them, and protected them. The first transcontinentals began as hybrid public/private enterprises and ended up as private corporations, but their public roots remained.”
- ¶10: the railroads helped create “the modern corporate lobby.”
- ¶12: “It was not ‘capital’ that built the railroads but credit, and the capital that was ultimately at risk in the railroads did not belong to the men who controlled them.”
- **¶22 (mechanism):** “the transcontinentals’ simultaneous failure as businesses and success as sources of individual fortunes for insiders … corporate containers for financial manipulation and political networking … The financiers made money through subsidies, the sale of securities, insider companies for the construction of the railroads themselves, and land speculation. Each funneled corporate resources into private pockets. To do this, they needed considerable […]”
- ¶24: the network of “friends”: “Corporations used the federal government to punish rival corporations while gaining advantages for themselves. They made politics a realm of private competition.”
- ¶33: names Leland Stanford among the promoters; “They were, however, not that smart … there is a Sorcerer’s Apprentice quality to them.”
- ¶35: written over about 12 years while teaching at the University of Washington and Stanford.
- **¶37 (Cardinal thesis line):** “At Stanford, itself a monument to a railroad fortune, I noticed something else. I came to the Silicon Valley in the midst of the dot.com boom at a time when very many people were becoming very rich by creating companies, or owning the securities of companies, that lost vast amounts of money … Eventually, I came to think of these […]”
- ¶40: antimonopolism “was racist to its core” in the West.

## Ch. 1 “Genesis” (¶1–105) — CORE: Associates, 1864 Act, land grants, insider construction companies
- Epigraph ¶1–2, Newton Booth: “It is easier, more delightful, and more profitable to build with other peoples’ money than our own.” (Source n100: Booth’s Aug. 1, 1874 speech, in Crane ed.)
- ¶3–23 cover Civil War railroading: Tom Scott’s corruption (systematic bribery of the Pennsylvania legislature over the tonnage tax, ¶12), war rates, Fink on fixed costs, standard gauge (Lincoln 1863, ¶23). Background only.
- ¶25–45 cover Jay Cooke and Salmon Chase, the bond-selling model, private favors (¶33–37) and a securities primer (Fisk & Hatch). This is the template for Gilded Age “friendship.” Background.
- ¶48: Senator Henry Wilson: “the liberality of this government, either by money or land.” This led to “hothouse capitalism.”
- ¶50: Theodore Judah, Central Pacific chief engineer, was also clerk of the House subcommittee on the Pacific railway bill and secretary of the Senate Pacific Railroad committee. He “used these positions to distribute Central Pacific stock, with a par or face value of $66,000, where he thought it could do the most good.” [n43]
- **¶51:** “a collection of Sacramento storekeepers who called themselves the Associates and whose net worth was probably no more than $350,000.” [n44] Huntington organized them late in 1860. The core five were Huntington, Leland Stanford, Mark Hopkins and the Crocker brothers (Charles and Edwin). They also built the Dutch Flat toll wagon road as a hedge.
- **¶53:** initial investment was “$1,500 apiece for all of them except Edwin Crocker,” plus $1,500 from James Bailey, so $7,500 was 10% down on 750 shares. Each Associate later bought 345 more shares. White’s estimate of the total combined investment is “$19,800.” Huntington used assessments in 1862 to threaten to force out Bailey and Judah. (Note-number glitch in the ebook: [n48] appears twice; the first should be n46.)
- **¶62:** in seeking the 1864 Act, “Huntington and Durant offered congressmen and others private favors to secure a public bounty. Durant and his allies distributed $250,000 in bonds … This was almost certainly the occasion upon which the Central Pacific gave some of its convertible bonds … to the men Mark Hopkins called ‘our friends of influence.’ [n59: Hopkins to CPH, Feb. 16, 1864, CPH Papers] […]”
- ¶63–65: government bonds were reduced to a **second** mortgage, and the companies were allowed an equal amount of first-mortgage bonds. Courts later held that interest was not due until maturity, so “for thirty years the government, not the railroads, would pay the interest.” White values the gift to the Union Pacific at about $43,000,000 in addition to the $77,000,000 loan.
- **¶66–68 (land):** the 1864 Act doubled the grant to 12,800 acres per mile plus coal and iron. Odd sections formed a checkerboard, and the price of the public sections was doubled to $2.50/acre. “The main line of the Central Pacific got slightly more than the landmass of Maryland.” Federal grants to all land-grant railroads totaled 131,230,358 acres (“Railroadiana”, third-largest state). State grants added 44,224,175 acres (33 million of them from Texas).
- ¶69: the land “belonged to Indians.” The Kickapoo Treaty is the case: Senator Pomeroy steered surplus lands to his own railroad (Twain’s Senator Dilworthy).
- ¶70: delays in issuing patents meant localities “could not easily tax railroad lands.”
- ¶71: the 1864 Act set no meeting point, so construction became “a race for subsidies.”
- ¶75: the March 1865 amendment allowed 100 miles of bonds in advance of construction. The Central Pacific made some of them convertible. The par-payment requirement was “never enforced.”
- **¶76:** under California’s General Railroad Law (stockholder liability and borrowing limited to capital stock), the Central Pacific issued stock “to the construction companies owned by the same men who controlled the Central Pacific … The best estimates are that at most $100,000 was paid for shares of the Central Pacific. The company’s annual report to the secretary of state of California that claimed $40 million in paid stock subscriptions in 1869 was fraudulent.” [n74: 1869 Annual Report, California State Archives]
- ¶77: “rule number one … put little or no money down … rule number two: negotiate among yourselves,” through the insider construction company.
- **¶79:** Charles Crocker & Co. was the “primitive Crédit Mobilier.” Hopkins, Feb. 1866: “[H]aving reached the present position [with] so little [stock] in outside hands, I think now it will pay us best to issue as little as possible & calculate to work it into the contractor & make it bring par or over within three years when the annual earnings of the road will be very large.” [n76: Hopkins to CPH, Feb. 16, 1866]
- **¶80:** the Contract and Finance Company was incorporated in 1867. “Its nominal incorporators actually held stock for the five Associates, who never paid anything for it. Instead, they gave their notes for the stock.” The Pacific Railway Commission estimated the Central Pacific “paid roughly twice the actual cost of construction per mile.” In 1868 the company got half of its $16,512,000 payment in gold and half in Central Pacific stock. Huntington, years later: “as rotten a corporation as ever lived.” [n77: CPH to H. E. Huntington, Jan. 5, 1898]
- **¶81 (Stanford and the Chinese):** “Leland Stanford, the president of the Central Pacific, had tried to exclude Chinese—the ‘dregs of Asia’—from California while governor … Chinese labor proved to be the Central Pacific’s salvation.”
- ¶85–86: Hopkins considered stopping at the California line. They jumped ahead into Nevada for the bonds. E. B. Crocker would “tremble for the future” (Feb. 1867).
- **¶94:** “when threatened with a congressional investigation, the books disappeared, never to resurface.” [n99: PRC 74] By Pacific Railway Commission figures, the bonds “roughly matched the cost of the road … more than enough to build the road without any substantial investment from the Associates.”

Carr, ‘Boss Billy,’ one of Leland Stanford’s political fixers, who also acted as an intermediary in a huge sale of Southern Pacific lands.”** **This ties a Stanford political operative directly to railroad-grant land.** (Ch3 ¶29: Carr, an “intimate of Stanford,” got $60k in bonds.)
- ¶8–12: railroads aimed migration like “a fire hose.” Mills (1891): the Sacramento Valley lost 20,000 of its natural increase, 1880–90.
- **¶13:** Stanford before the PRC (1887): “It [the Central Pacific] was the first enterprise anywhere in the world which made possible the habitation of regions of country far remote from navigable waters, and has added untold millions to the wealth of the nation.” [n15: Stanford testimony, July 28, 1887, **PRC 7:2465**] **CITATION INCONSISTENCY:** ch8 n106 gives Stanford’s July 28 start as **PRC 5:2461**; volume 5 vs 7 for nearly the same page. Log it. Mills (Dec. 1893): the Central Pacific, California & Oregon, and Oregon & California had disposed of only 20% of their grants, with **12,610,512 acres remaining of 15,653,000 granted**. [n17: Mills to CPH, Dec. 22, 1893]
- ¶17–31: bison slaughter as “dumb growth.” The Northern Pacific’s hide traffic was about 1/3 of 1% of total. Off-topic for Cardinal; read in full.
- ¶32–72: the open-range cattle industry (book counts, the Great Die-Up of 1886–87, illegal fencing of the public domain). ¶48: “It seemed no more necessary for the promoters of cattle corporations to know anything about raising cattle than for Leland Stanford or Collis P. Huntington to know anything about railroads.” Otherwise off-topic.
- ¶73–86: the North vs. South Dakota “laboratory”: unsubsidized roads produced denser, faster settlement, “a compelling argument against land grants.” This is relevant to Cardinal framing on the cost of land grants.
- ¶87–99: “rain follows the plow,” the 1889 Sioux land cession, the Canadian Pacific. ¶96: “in California, the Southern Pacific encouraged farmers to turn to fruit.”
- ¶101–102: White disagrees with Mercer’s social-return estimates for the Central Pacific and Union Pacific. Mills noted that speculators and higher prices slowed settlement.
- ¶103–105: real per-capita income from labor in much of the West in 1900 was below 1880.
- **¶106:** “Collis P. Huntington died in 1900 with an estate valued at roughly $50 million … Huntington’s was only a quarter share of the Southern Pacific Railroad fortune. **Assuming that the families of the other Associates had done as well, they had collectively accumulated $200 million.** Were the Associates and the railroads they controlled worth this?” [n149: Thorpe, *H. E. Huntington*, 157] Note this is White’s extrapolation (“Assuming”), not a measured Stanford figure.

## Interlude dm11 “Mise en scène: Wovoka” (¶1–8)
- Currier & Ives’ *Across the Continent* (1868). In 1890 Lakota and other Ghost Dance delegates rode the Oregon Short Line and the **Central Pacific** across Nevada to Wovoka. “Pueblos helped build the Southern Pacific.” Indigenous context; no Stanford content. Peripheral.

## Epilogue (¶1–21)
- The Civil War generation built railroads “whose accounts would never bear examining.” Adams and Villard skipped their railroad lives in their memoirs.
- **¶8:** Huntington’s 1899 letter to James Speyer and his Nordhoff sketch were attempts “to settle old scores, particularly with his Associate Leland Stanford, whom he regarded as a burden and an embarrassment.” (This is the source behind ch6 n115/n134/n136: CPH to Speyer, Dec. 6, 1899.)
- ¶9: Huntington “cited as proof of his virtue his victories in litigation, as dubious a proof in nineteenth-century America as it is possible to imagine.”
- ¶13: Huntington died in 1900, leaving his fortune to Arabella, her son and his nephew Henry, the source of the Huntington Library.
- ¶20: Adams: successful men were “a set of mere money-getters and traders.”

## Conclusion (¶1–26)
- **¶6:** “Profit arose more from financial markets and insider contracts than from successfully selling transportation.”
- ¶7: modernity as “the triumph of the unfit, whose survival demanded the intervention of the state, which the corporations themselves corrupted.”
- ¶10–13: railroads and the state were “coproductions.” Congress picked winners and losers through land grants and rescissions, investigations, sinking funds, taxes, rights of way. “Politics still offers a way for corporations to compete.”
- ¶22: the “tax on trade”: “A shipper in 1885 was still paying for the frauds of the 1860s.”
- **¶23:** “the dimmer lights among them, such as Leland Stanford, had to have so much explained to them.”
- ¶26: the transcontinentals should not have been built “when and where they were built.”

## Appendix and abbreviations (BM03–BM04)
- Every map and chart was produced by the **Spatial History Lab, Stanford University**. Map C covers Southern Pacific/Central Pacific land grants in the Central Valley. White’s fuller annotated notes are on the Stanford Spatial History Project website.
- **Archival note for Cardinal:** the key Associates archives White used are at Stanford: the **Leland Stanford Papers (SC33a)**, **Pacific Improvement Company Records 1869–1931**, the Timothy Hopkins Transportation Collection (M0097), the Hyde, Ives and Plumb papers, Ralston correspondence and the Stephen M. White Papers. The Central Pacific vouchers (MS 10) are at the California State Railroad Museum. PRC = 50th Cong., 1st sess., S. Ex. Doc. 51, 10 vols. Also listed: the Colton case depositions and testimony (Colton v. Stanford, Sonoma Co. Superior Court, 1883–84).

### Connections to Cardinal people / threads
1. **Railroad → land → Hoover (spine tie).** Hoover's first employer was a land-speculation company that existed because "it was only when the transcontinental rail link was formed that full-blown settlement occurred and land prices boomed, creating the opportunity on which Minthorn and his partners intended to capitalize" (p. 26). The firm also owned the Salem Street Railway (p. 28). Its investors "drew few distinctions between the public's interest and their own" (p. 27). Hoover was among the first Americans to ride the newly opened rail route to Oregon (pp. 19–20).
2. **Yale thread: Louis Janin** — "educated at Yale and Freiburg," Comstock Lode and Rothschilds (p. 46). Janin's recommendation sent Hoover to Bewick, Moreing (p. 49). Lunch "likely at the Pacific Union Club on Nob Hill" (p. 47), Whyte's inference.
3. **Public story vs. documented conduct (Janin hire).** Hoover's memoir tells a charming copyist-to-engineer story. Whyte says the real hire rested on Hoover's usefulness to the North Star defense: he published a supposedly objective article in *Mining & Scientific Press* that matched North Star's case, without disclosing his tie to Janin, and was paid right after the verdict (pp. 47–48).
4. **Panic of 1893 as hinge.** It wiped out Minthorn's Oregon Land Co. and cost Hoover his USGS job (p. 45), the same downturn that hits Stanford's estate after Leland's death (cross-check with White, *Who Killed Jane Stanford?*). Whyte's frame: Hoover was "conceived in one economic depression" and "graduated into another" (p. 45).
5. **Grant's Quaker Policy / Indian agents in the family.** Guardian Lawrie Tatum was "one of President Grant's first Indian Agents," author of *Our Red Brothers* (p. 25 n.*³). Uncle Laban Miles was Osage agent (p. 16). A possible tie to Cardinal's land-dispossession thread. Moderate.
6. **Branner patronage line.** Hoover was office assistant from his second semester (p. 36). Branner arranged the Ozarks and Lindgren summers (pp. 37, 39–40) and advised him to turn down USGS for commercial mining (p. 48). Branner's own Edison and Boston-gold-mining past (p. 48).
7. **Stanford enrollment corroboration.** "registered his 558 classmates" (p. 35) makes 559 with Hoover. That matches White's 559 and is a third data point for the 555 vs. 559 open issue (drafts/v0.1/OPEN_ISSUES.md).
8. **Benjamin Harrison at Stanford** (p. 38). A former president was on campus during Hoover's years. Harrison's Stanford law lectures (1894) are NOT in Whyte; verify elsewhere before use.
9. **Labor practices foreshadowing Gwalia/Kaiping.** He lengthened Coolgardie shifts "from forty-four to forty-eight hours," fired strikers and hired "more pliable Italian labor" (p. 55), and fired a 72-year-old bookkeeper after raising $300 for him (p. 55).
10. **Route to Kaiping / Leopold–Francqui thread.** Moreing, "recently returned from a tour of China, had agreed to provide the imperial mining administrator at Tientsin with loans and engineering expertise" (p. 65). That is the bridge to the Kaiping/Belgian thread in the timeline (1901 memorandum).

### CONTRADICTIONS with our draft (checked against GitHub kylesmcauliffe/cardinal @ 63a999e, Nov 21 2026)
1. **Swain's department.** `books/cardinal/ch/3-01-stanford-prototype-hoover.qmd` l.125 calls Swain "A Stanford geology professor named Joseph Swain [who] came through Portland recruiting." Whyte p. 33: Swain was "a professor in Stanford's inaugural math department" who "administered the Portland exams." Whyte has Hoover going to Portland to take the exams, not Swain coming to recruit. **STRONG: fix.**
2. **"Passed mathematics and failed everything else."** In 3-01 l.127, rewrite `chapters/ep4-03-farm-opening-day.md` l.13 ("failing every entrance subject except mathematics") and podcast ep05. Whyte p. 33: "he struggled and came up short… Bert was admitted on condition that he bone up on geometry". On campus "He studied hard, took his exams, and failed again, this time in English" (p. 35). Whyte makes geometry the condition, so math was not cleanly passed. Whyte praises his *tenacity* at plane geometry, not a pass. **STRONG: reconcile or attribute (the line appears to come from Harris or the repo ch 3-01; check Harris ch 2.3).**
3. **"Swain admitted him."** `drafts/v0.1/part-04` l.100 and podcast ep04 l.116. Whyte p. 33 says Stanford ("Stanford, in need of students to fill its dormitories") admitted him, not Swain personally. Minor wording.
4. **"His first job after graduating was pushing ore carts in a Nevada mine."** In 3-01 l.159, rewrite `ep5-01-gwalia.md` l.27, and podcast ep05. Whyte pp. 45–46: the Reward Mine at **Nevada City / Grass Valley, California** (Nevada County), not the state of Nevada. Whyte also says his last USGS summer with Lindgren came *after* senior year (pp. 39–41), so the mine was not strictly his first post-graduation job. **Fix wording to "a Grass Valley (Nevada County, Calif.) mine."**
5. **"In 1897, at twenty-three, he was sent to Western Australia."** In 3-01 and ep5-01. He left SF Mar 24, 1897 and reached Albany in May 1897 (pp. 50, 54), and was born Aug 10, 1874 (p. 4). So he was **22** when sent; Whyte p. 49 says "twenty-two years of age" at the Oct 1896 offer. The ep5-01 opener "August 1897… Hoover was twenty-three" is fine (he turned 23 on Aug 10). Minor.

Red House, Hornton Street, Campden Hill, Kensington (p. 106). Open door for Californians and Stanford alumni. 1908–14 remembered as perhaps his happiest years (p. 105).

### Books II–V and Epilogue — Cardinal threads (chs 7–27, pp. 128–614)

Whyte’s later books are the war, the Commerce years, the presidency, and the long afterlife. Below are the threads that touch the Cardinal web. The presidency itself (chs 18–24) was surveyed, not line-by-line transcribed.

#### CRB and Francqui (chs 7–9, especially pp. 141–144, 147–149, 167–168)
- Sept 1914: Belgian **Comité Central de Secours et d’Alimentation** sends **Millard Shaler** to London; he arrives Sept 26 to buy $100,000 of food (p. 141). Hoover meets him “on or about October 6” (p. 142).
- Oct 10: Hoover tells Ambassador Page he is considering schemes; within forty-eight hours he is back with a plan. Page convenes a meeting including **Emile Francqui**, chairman of the Comité Central (pp. 142–143).
- p. 143, verbatim: “Francqui was one of the richest men in Belgium and a former lieutenant for King Leopold II in the Congo.” “Francqui was known to Hoover. They had overlapped for six months in China, with Francqui representing Moreing’s Belgian partners in the Chinese Engineering and Mining Company. They had not gotten along but now put aside their differences in the ambassador’s presence.”
- p. 144: Page’s summit “culminated in the founding of the Committee for the Relief of Belgium (CRB).” Hoover’s informal charter is a letter to Page **dated October 20**. Hoover chairs the CRB; Francqui’s Comité handles distribution in Belgium. (Ledger dates the organization 1914-10-01, a month placeholder. Whyte’s document date is October 20. Draft fix: use mid-to-late October / the October 20 letter, not October 1.)
- Naming: Whyte uses “Comité Central” at the founding; the ledger uses “Comité National de Secours et d’Alimentation.” Record both; do not treat as a hard contradiction (the Brussels committee is often later called the Comité National).
- First gift ship, 3,500 tons, arrives in Holland Nov 21 (p. 147). Francqui organizes distribution to Belgium’s 2,633 communes (p. 147). Need quickly rises from Hoover’s ~20,000 tons/month estimate to Francqui’s cable of at least 80,000 tons; prewar Belgian grain imports ~250,000 tons/month; cost from $1 million/month to at least $4 million (p. 148).
- Later, “for the better part of a year,” Hoover and Francqui “engaged in a near-psychotic quarrel for preeminence” (p. 167). Hoover “talked of laying a train of powder to blow up Francqui, and at another threatened to train a machine gun on the ‘glory hunting Belgian pinheads.’” Eustace Percy’s late November 1916 warning fails. They settle at the Savoy in London at the end of December: Francqui accuses Hoover of using a sledgehammer to kill gnats; Hoover replies that he would “use a pile driver to kill a malarial mosquito.” (pp. 167–168).
- p. 211 is the **Order of Leopold** (a Belgian honor offered by King Albert), not King Leopold II. Leopold II appears in this book, after p. 65, only at p. 143 (Francqui in the Congo). Whyte does **not** narrate Leopold’s Kaiping share purchases or de Wouters/Thys; those remain with Nash and Carlson.

#### Colorado River / Boulder / Hoover Dam

The later flourish is imprecise; do not let it drag the first job back into “Nevada” or the Colorado country.
- Whyte does **not** narrate Interior Secretary Wilbur’s 17 Sept 1930 naming, or the organization of Six Companies / Bechtel and Kaiser (ledger 1930-09-17, 1931-02-01). Those remain with Stevens, McCartney, Denton.
- p. 587: after WWII, “the administration was reconsidering the name of the Boulder Dam. It had initially been called the Hoover Dam. Roosevelt’s spiteful secretary of the interior, Harold Ickes, had with his president’s approval changed it to Boulder Dam. Congress, with Truman’s support, changed it back in 1947, in part because it was deserved, and also as a reward to Hoover for his service.”

**Citation scheme:** print page from Liveright ebook page_N anchors [[p. N]] + ¶ within chapter; notes in extract.

- **Method (lean mode, Nov 21, 2026):**
  - Close-read ch. 4, "The Conspiracy for Corporate Rights" (pp. 112–160), and its notes 1–73. This is the Stanford / Southern Pacific / Field chapter.

## Run 1 — 2026-11-21 — Lean mode: ch 4 (pp. 112–160) + notes 1–73 close-read; rest keyword-skimmed

## Top findings for Cardinal
1. **San Mateo (Dec 20, 1882): Conkling's "secret journal"** (CANON-116).
   - The Southern Pacific's lawyer, a former senator and the last surviving member of the Joint Committee on Reconstruction, told the Court that the drafters chose "persons" to cover corporations. He cited the committee's unpublished journal.
   - Graham, *Everyman's Constitution*: "a deliberate, brazen forgery."
   - The Court never decided the case. About two years later Stanford's railroad paid the taxes and settled (pp. 113–143).
2. **The test-case campaign** (CANON-119).
   - The 1879 constitution taxed railroads without the mortgage deduction.
   - The SP and CP refused to pay, ran a press campaign, and brought about 63 test cases (Daily Alta, Feb. 10, 1886).
   - Team: Sanderson, Edmunds, Pomeroy, and Conkling (pp. 119–120).
3. **Field as Stanford's judge** (CANON-118).
   - Field recommended Pomeroy, then presided over the same cases on circuit.
   - He wrote "the very essence of tyranny" and leaked other justices' confidential memoranda to the railroad's lawyers.
   - Waite refused to give him a Central Pacific opinion because of his "intimate personal relations with the managers."
   - Stanford "was even said to be behind" Field's nomination (pp. 140–142).
4. **Santa Clara (May 10, 1886, 118 U.S. 394): the fence holding vs. Davis's headnote** (CANON-117).
   - Waite's note to Davis: "we avoided the constitutional question in the decision."
   - Davis printed the remark and a personhood headnote anyway; he had once been president of the Newburgh and New York Railway.
   - Field turned the headnote into precedent in Beckwith (1889): "It was so held in Santa Clara…" (pp. 144–157).
5. **Outcome framing.** Collins (1912): of 604 Fourteenth Amendment cases, 312 involved corporations and 28 involved African Americans. "Magna Charta of accumulated and organized capital" (p. 158ff.). This is already in the ep03 review.

## Conflicts with the Cardinal drafts (and what was done)
- The drafts already use Winkler accurately: ep03 "The Caption"; timeline l.42–43; ledger 1886-05-10; ep03 review l.59–66. No date changes were needed.
- ep03 narration paraphrased Field as comparing the railroad's property to "a widow's property." Field's actual comparison was white/black and old/young owners. **Fixed** to "anyone else's" in the md, narration and spoken copies. The audio is not regenerated.
- outline.md l.163 said "Check Winkler, which isn't downloaded yet." **Resolved** with a note. l.210 status updated.
- The ep03 review's l.84 note is confirmed: Stoneman's "natural person / artificial person" lines are not in Winkler.

## Do not import from Winkler
- "When Stanford established [the university] … in 1891, he asked Field to be one of its founding trustees." Field was named in the Founding Grant of Nov 11, 1885 (CANON-097, CANON-118).
- The 1861 "suitcase full of Central Pacific stock certificates" and the "$500,000 annually" in bribes. Both are unverified, with secondary cites only (CANON-120).
- "Stanford drove in the famous Golden Spike." He swung and missed at the ceremony (Chang; CANON-091).

## Ivory crossovers
- **Elihu Yale and the East India Company** (p. 26; Conclusion pp. 382–383: Yale "named after Elihu Yale, one of the stockholders made rich by the East India Company"). Matches the expansion-plan Yale formula.
- **Dartmouth College case** (ch. 3): colleges as corporations, the legal frame for a Founding Grant.
- Graham's 1938 *Yale Law Journal* article "Four Letters of Mr. Justice Field" is the source for Field's leaks to the SP.
- No Harriman, Bones or Dulles material.

## Leads for other books
- **White, *Railroaded*:** the JAH 2003 article and CP lobbying sums. Check the "$500,000 a year" figure.
- **Rayner:** the Conkling/SP retainer; Stanford's motives for settling San Mateo.
- **Harris:** Field–Stanford; Sharon/Terry (Field presided in 1888 per Winkler p. 137, consistent with lead-chase CANON-098, where Field was not on the 1885 panel).
